framework.summary: An executable methodology for enterprise PQC migration — not a whitepaper, checklist, or vendor pitch. Structured as an 8-phase lifecycle (Phase 0 through Phase 7) with cross-cutting concerns woven throughout. Described as the first published PQC migration methodology covering the complete migration lifecycle at operational depth in a single integrated framework (a survey of 80+ published PQC frameworks found no other single framework covers this full scope; organizations otherwise combine four or five separate frameworks). Informed by but not derivative of NIST FIPS 203/204/205, NIST IR 8547, NIST SP 1800-38, NIST SP 800-227, NSA CNSA 2.0, the PQCC Migration Roadmap, the Dutch PQC Migration Handbook, GSMA PQ.01–PQ.03, ETSI TR 103 619 / TR 104 016, and the PKI Consortium PQCMM. Key differentiators include the Minimum Viable CBOM model, risk-driven discovery scoping, emphasis on vendor governance as the primary external constraint on timelines, and an integrated operational security architecture (SOC and GRC).

intro.how_to_use: An executable methodology, not a whitepaper, checklist, or vendor pitch. Structured as an 8-phase lifecycle (Phase 0 through Phase 7) with cross-cutting concerns woven throughout. Each phase defines: Prerequisites (what must be in place before you start); Activities (what you do, with enough specificity to assign to a team next Monday); Decision Points (where choices branch based on your context); Outputs (what you produce, with quality criteria); Interdependencies (what feeds into and out of this phase); Common Failures (what goes wrong and how to avoid it); and Maturity Indicators (how to assess whether you've done this phase well enough to proceed). Organizations should not expect to execute phases sequentially in a clean waterfall — real programs overlap (e.g. running Phase 1 discovery on some systems while executing Phase 5 pilots on others). The phase structure provides a logical dependency order; the calendar comes from the Phase 4 roadmap.
intro.architecture_at_a_glance: Phases are logically sequential but operationally overlapping: real programs run discovery, documentation, pilots, and vendor engagement concurrently.

regulatory_timeline_context.note: The framework is designed to satisfy converging deadlines. The regulatory table mixes binding requirements, recommended roadmaps, and planning milestones at varying stages of finalization; not every date is legally binding. Implication: organizations starting now have 4–9 years depending on jurisdiction and system criticality; a credibly planned migration for a large enterprise requires 4–15 years of execution. There is no slack in the schedule.

phases.name: Phase 0 — Executive Mandate & Business Case
phases.cadence: sequential (the only phase that must be substantially complete before others begin)
phases.summary: Establish the governance foundation and secure multi-year funding, authority, and organizational commitment. Frames PQC migration as a multi-year enterprise transformation program (not an IT project) and is the single most common failure point.
phases.overlaps_with: Late-stage Phase 0 activities (governance finalization, detailed budget approval) can overlap with early Phase 1 discovery on the highest-priority systems; experienced organizations run a lightweight 'Phase 0.5' concurrently to scope the top 10–20 critical systems and top 10 vendor dependencies.

activities.title: Frame the Business Case
activities.do: Structure the executive argument around four concrete, current 'urgency drivers' rather than speculative Q-Day predictions.
activities.detail: The four urgency drivers: (1) Regulatory and compliance deadlines — map exposure to the timeline table; e.g. PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 12.3.3 (annual review of all crypto cipher suites/protocols), NIS2 and DORA for EU operations, CNSA 2.0 for government suppliers. (2) Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) exposure — data with 10+ year confidentiality requirements (trade secrets, M&A plans, health records, national security info, long-lived financial instruments, attorney-client communications); risk is active now. (3) Trust Now, Forge Later (TNFL) exposure — long-lived signatures/trust anchors (PKI roots often 20+ year validity, code-signing keys, firmware signing keys, legal/regulatory document signatures, OT safety certificates). (4) Client, investor, and insurer expectations — fiduciary duty, investor due diligence, cyber insurance underwriting, procurement requirements. Decision Point: data with >10-year confidentiality AND regulated industry → HNDL alone justifies immediate action; signature-integrity primary risk (OT/ICS, PKI operators) → TNFL drives urgency on different systems.

activities.title: Build the Budget Structure
activities.do: Structure funding as a multi-year program with phased investment rather than a single project budget line, and align spend to existing infrastructure refresh cycles.
activities.detail: Year 1 (Foundation): inventory and discovery tooling, initial CBOM development, 2–3 hybrid pilots, vendor engagement, policy updates, team training; illustrative range for a large enterprise $1.5M–$4M (varies by estate complexity/tooling). Years 2–3 (Bulk Migration): rollout to Tier-1 systems, PKI modernization, key-lifetime reductions, dual-signing pilots, vendor upgrade coordination; most capital-intensive phase. Years 4–5 (Long Tail and Hardening): embedded/OT systems, legacy containment, eliminating compensating controls, crypto-agility maturation. Key budget strategy: align spending to existing refresh cycles (data center refreshes, SD-WAN upgrades, cloud migrations, PKI renewals, vendor contract renewals) to avoid big-bang spikes. The 'umbrella program' strategy positions quantum readiness as the organizing framework for long-overdue security modernization (PKI, certificate lifecycle, HSMs, asset inventories, vendor governance). Align with innovation/R&D/digitization budgets; position PQC as a mandatory security track within broader programs rather than competing for separate allocation.

activities.title: Build the Business Case — Additional Benefit Arguments
activities.do: Beyond the four urgency drivers, marshal additional arguments that strengthen the business case.
activities.detail: Regulatory trust and approval acceleration — a mature quantum readiness posture (documented CBOM, risk assessment, migration roadmap) signals proactive technology-risk management to regulators and can reduce friction during supervisory review of new products/services (depends on sector, jurisdiction, regulator). Immediate security value from cryptographic inventory — a quantum-vulnerability-focused inventory surfaces classically vulnerable cryptography (deprecated TLS 1.0/1.1, weak keys RSA-1024/DH-1024, insecure cipher suites RC4/3DES/export ciphers, expired/misconfigured certificates, hardcoded keys, unpatched libraries with CVEs, downgrade-allowing protocols) remediable immediately; makes the Phase 1 investment self-funding from a security perspective. Competitive differentiation and market access — quantum resilience becomes a market signal; procurement increasingly includes quantum readiness criteria. Security talent attraction and retention — PQC and crypto-agility expertise is scarce; a serious program offers frontier work and is a recruiting/retention asset.

activities.title: Develop Migration Cost Estimates
activities.do: Build a budget structure despite inherent imprecision; estimate each cost-driver category separately rather than waiting for precise data.
activities.detail: Cost Driver Taxonomy (eight categories): Discovery and inventory tooling (SandboxAQ, IBM Quantum Safe, Keyfactor, ISARA Advance, CryptoNext or equivalent, plus deployment/integration and ongoing license costs); Cryptographic engineering labor (typically the largest category; PQC talent scarce, premium rates); Vendor PQC licensing and upgrades (HSM firmware upgrades alone $50K–$500K+ depending on module count); HSM and hardware refresh (older HSMs may not support PQC key types; procurement lead times 6–12 months; budget hardware + commissioning, key ceremony, migration); PKI modernization (CA upgrades, automated certificate lifecycle management, root CA ceremonies, intermediate CA provisioning — required regardless of PQC for shorter certificate lifetimes); Performance and capacity uplift (CPU, memory, bandwidth, storage increases); Testing environments (production-mirror environments); Program management overhead (QRPM, PMO tools, SteerCo/working-group facilitation, training, vendor management, compliance tracking, board reporting). The Infrastructure Modernization Umbrella: combine independently justified investments (PKI automation for 47-day certificate lifetimes, FIPS 140-3 upgrades for FIPS 140-2 sunset, HSM refresh for EOL hardware, library/platform upgrades for CVEs) into a single 'cryptographic infrastructure modernization' program. Reference Program Economics (anchors from a published large global telco program, PostQuantum.com): discovery and inventory $2–5M for a large operator (~1 year); assessment/planning ~1–2% of total but determines whether the remaining 98% is spent in the right order; implementation dominates; steady-state ops a few million/year. Order of magnitude $300–500M over a decade for a major global telco vs U.S. federal civilian comparator $7.1B for 2025–2035 (OMB). Peak staffing dozens of FTEs (the telco model peaked around 50). Present gross program cost and net incremental cost separately.

activities.title: Establish Governance Structure
activities.do: Stand up the program's roles, workstreams, decision cadence, board oversight model, risk appetite statement, and three-lines-of-defense structure.
activities.detail: Roles: Executive Sponsor (CISO or CIO) — visible owner, clears roadblocks, briefs board quarterly, reports to Board/Risk Committee; Steering Committee (SteerCo) — cross-functional (Security, Enterprise Architecture, AppDev, Infrastructure/NetSec, PKI/Identity, Compliance/Legal, Procurement, Business Unit reps), reports monthly to Sponsor; Quantum Readiness Program Manager (QRPM) — day-to-day leader, runs plan/risk log/KPIs, reports weekly to SteerCo lead; Workstream Leads (one per domain) — execute phase activities, report weekly to QRPM. Eight workstreams: (1) Inventory & Discovery (Crypto-BOM ownership); (2) Network & TLS/VPN (hybrid rollouts); (3) PKI & Code Signing (roots, issuers, toolchains); (4) Applications & Platforms (libraries, service mesh, cloud); (5) Embedded/IoT/OT (gateways, compensating controls); (6) Policy/Compliance/Procurement (standards, clauses); (7) Vendor Orchestration (roadmaps, SLAs); (8) Education & Change Management (training, comms). Decision cadence: Weekly PMO; Monthly SteerCo; Quarterly Board/Risk Committee. Program leadership: the CISO should lead in most organizations (PQC is a security risk response, not a tech refresh); CIO co-sponsors and chairs technical workstreams. Board oversight runs through the existing risk/audit committee: initial briefing 60–90 min once during Phase 0; quarterly KPI review 15–20 min (five board KPIs — Coverage, Trust, Inventory, Vendors, Agility); annual risk appetite review; escalation triggers (material CRQC timeline change, program >6 months behind regulatory buffer, confirmed vulnerability in a deployed PQC algorithm, Tier 1 vendor abandoning PQC without alternative). Risk Appetite operates at strategic level plus operational tolerances (illustrative): HNDL ≤20% of >10-year secrecy data quantum-vulnerable by end of 2027, 0% by end of 2029; TNFL all production software/firmware signing using NIST-approved quantum-resistant signatures by end of 2027, all CA signing keys PQC-capable by end of 2029; Regulatory compliance ≥12 months before deadline; Crypto-agility mandatory for all systems deployed from Q3 2026. Three Lines of Defense: first line owns/executes; second line (CISO/risk/compliance, QRPM sits here) governs; third line (internal audit) provides assurance. SOC must develop detection for five quantum-related threat scenarios; GRC owns the risk appetite statement, KRI framework, regulatory intelligence, audit evidence dossier, insurance prep; the critical SOC/GRC handoff is the cryptographic inventory (a shared, machine-readable, SIEM-integrated asset — a Phase 1 architecture decision).

activities.title: Draft the Program Charter
activities.do: Produce a one-page charter document.
activities.detail: Covers: Purpose (quantum-safe migration and crypto-agility); Scope (TLS/VPN, PKI/code-signing, applications/platforms, embedded/OT, policy/procurement, vendors, training); Success criteria (stop new HNDL exposure; protect long-lived trust anchors; meet 2030/2035 regulatory timelines; embed crypto-agility as organizational capability); Cadence (weekly PMO; monthly SteerCo; quarterly board); Escalation path (sponsor decides on funding/dates; risk acceptance decisions documented and auditable).

activities.title: Conduct Initial Scoping Assessment
activities.do: Before launching full discovery, perform a rapid (2–4 week) scoping assessment to establish program boundaries.
activities.detail: (1) Identify the top 20 revenue-generating or mission-critical systems. (2) For each, determine primary cryptographic protocols in use, data sensitivity classification, number of dependent systems, vendor ownership vs internal control. (3) Estimate the approximate size of the cryptographic estate (TLS endpoints, certificates, VPN tunnels, HSM-protected keys, code-signing pipelines). (4) Identify the 5–10 vendors whose PQC readiness will most constrain the migration timeline. Becomes the input for Phase 1 prioritization and calibrates Year 1 budget and staffing.

common_failures.title: 'Innovation project' framing
common_failures.why: Treating PQC migration as an R&D initiative or skunkworks project instead of a funded, governed program guarantees it will be deprioritized when competing for resources with operational imperatives.

common_failures.title: Single-year budget
common_failures.why: Securing one year of funding and hoping to 'show results' to justify the next year. PQC migration is a 4–15 year program; without multi-year commitment, teams cannot plan realistically or retain specialized talent.

common_failures.title: Missing business unit representation on SteerCo
common_failures.why: The migration touches every application, integration, and vendor relationship; without business-unit buy-in at the governance level, workstream leads face constant political resistance.

common_failures.title: Delegating to vendors
common_failures.why: Assuming 'our vendors will sort this out' and not running an internal program. Vendors update products on their own timelines; without an internal program driving requirements, tracking commitments, and testing deployments, the organization has no control over its migration timeline. The single most dangerous misconception.

common_failures.title: Premature lockdown
common_failures.why: Reacting to quantum headlines or a regulator's inquiry by abruptly restricting data access or disabling systems. HNDL risk is not reduced by making data harder to use; already-harvested traffic is already gone, and knee-jerk restrictions burn operational goodwill the program will need for a decade. Channel urgency into the structured program instead.

gate.note: Phase 0 exit corresponds to the executive-mandate gate: charter approved, multi-year budget committed, governance structure (SteerCo confirmed, QRPM appointed, cadence established), initial scoping assessment, and board briefing delivered.

phases.name: Phase 1 — Discovery & Inventory
phases.cadence: iterative / continuous (transitions from project-mode initial discovery into a permanent continuous-discovery capability; never fully ends in mature programs)
phases.summary: Build a comprehensive, continuously updated inventory of all cryptographic usage across IT, OT, cloud, IoT, and third-party systems. Foundational activity on which every subsequent phase depends — you cannot migrate what you cannot see. Major organizations should plan 12–24 months of dedicated team effort; no single tool provides 100% discovery.
phases.overlaps_with: Runs in parallel with Phase 2 from an early stage (CBOM data structure defined before large-scale discovery so inventory populates the CBOM directly); also generates early inputs for Phase 7 (vendor dependency data) and Phase 3 (first risk-relevant metadata); and runs in parallel with itself indefinitely as continuous discovery.

activities.title: Risk-Driven Scoping — Decide What to Inventory First
activities.do: Apply an 80/20 prioritization to determine where to focus initial discovery effort before launching broad discovery; an architecture-first approach concentrating discovery where risk concentrates.
activities.detail: Step 1 — Identify Tier-1 systems using existing organizational knowledge (revenue data, business impact assessments, regulatory scope documents, incident history, architecture diagrams): top 20–50 systems by business criticality. Step 2 — Classify by exposure type: Internet-exposed flows (external TLS, partner VPNs, email gateways) → immediate HNDL risk; long-lived secrecy data with confidentiality requirement >10 years → highest HNDL value; long-lived trust anchors with signature validity 5+ years (PKI roots, code-signing, firmware signing) → TNFL risk. Step 3 — Assign discovery priority tiers: Priority A (internet-exposed + long-lived secrecy data or trust anchors) discover first, target 30–60 days; Priority B (internal Tier-1 with significant data sensitivity) discover next, target 60–120 days; Priority C (everything else) discover on an ongoing basis, target 6–12 months. Delivers 70–80% of risk coverage with 20–30% of total discovery effort; Priority A output is sufficient to begin Phase 2 CBOM population and Phase 3 risk scoring.

activities.title: Establish Three Parallel Inventory Tracks
activities.do: Run integrated discovery across three interdependent domains coordinated through a single governance structure, even if executed by different teams with different tools.
activities.output: Cryptographic asset inventory; Sensitive data map (integrated); Systems and assets register (integrated)
activities.detail: Track A — Cryptographic Inventory: all uses of cryptography (algorithms, key sizes, protocols, libraries, certificate chains, key lifetimes). Track B — Sensitive Data Discovery and Classification: catalogs sensitive data by confidentiality requirements and retention periods; determines HNDL urgency. Track C — Systems and Assets Inventory: hardware/software assets, criticality, vendor ownership, lifecycle status; determines feasibility/sequencing. The intersection of all three enables defensible Phase 3 prioritization. Confidentiality horizons (Track B): for each data category assign a horizon in order of precedence: (1) statutory/regulatory retention (health 10–30y, audit/tax 7–10y), (2) contractual confidentiality (NDA survival), (3) IP lifetime (trade secrets 15y+), (4) business value decay (M&A 2–5y, strategic plans 3–7y, pricing 1–3y). Longest horizon governs; record on each data store; Phase 3 Dimension 1 consumes it. Resist classifying everything as long-lived.

activities.title: Deploy Cryptographic Discovery — Layered Approach
activities.do: Deploy a combination of discovery techniques because no single technique covers all cryptographic usage; supplement with tool selection across capability categories.
activities.detail: Five layers: Layer 1 Network Traffic Analysis (passive monitoring captures TLS/SSH/IPsec handshakes — cipher suites, certificate chains, key sizes, protocol versions; cannot see encrypted payloads or data at rest). Layer 2 Static Code Analysis (scan repos for crypto API calls, hardcoded algorithms, library imports; cannot detect runtime/dynamically loaded crypto or third-party binaries without source). Layer 3 Configuration and Certificate Scanning (enumerate certs from cert mgmt + CT logs, scan network device configs, query cloud KMS metadata; shows configured policy not runtime negotiation). Layer 4 Runtime and Binary Analysis (for systems without source — vendor appliances, legacy binaries, embedded firmware; requires specialized skills). Layer 5 Manual Investigation (interviews, architecture docs, vendor security docs, HSM/KMS usage logs; catches custom/proprietary/embedded crypto; labor-intensive). Tool categories: (1) Dedicated Cryptographic Discovery Platforms (CBOM output — SandboxAQ, IBM, Keyfactor [acquired InfoSec Global, CipherInsights], ISARA Advance, CryptoNext, Palo Alto Networks); (2) Network Traffic Analysis; (3) SAST with crypto detection; (4) SCA/SBOM; (5) Certificate/PKI Discovery (incl. CT logs); (6) CSPM; (7) Binary Analysis/Reverse Engineering; (8) Extract crypto metadata from existing security tools (SIEM, vuln scanners — rapid baseline); (9) AI-Assisted Analysis (emerged 2026; ~92% functional correctness reported on crypto code migration; treat findings as candidates requiring verification). Recommendation: deploy Categories 1–2, supplement with 7/8 for hard-to-reach systems, manual investigation (Layer 5) for the top 20 critical systems; prioritize tools producing CycloneDX CBOM.

activities.title: Map the Cryptographic Estate
activities.do: For every cryptographic instance discovered, record a standard set of fields.
activities.detail: Fields per instance: System/Asset ID (linked to CMDB); Cryptographic Function (key exchange, signing, encryption at rest); Algorithm (RSA-2048, ECDHE-P256, AES-256-GCM); Key Size (bits); Protocol (TLS 1.2, SSH 2.0, IPsec IKEv2); Library/Implementation (OpenSSL 3.0.12, BoringSSL, Java 17 JCA); Certificate Details (issuer, validity, chain depth); Key Lifetime (ephemeral, 1 year, 20-year root); Data Sensitivity (Confidential/Restricted/Public); Quantum Vulnerability (Shor, Grover, or neither); Owner; Vendor Dependency; Control Posture (Full/Partial/No control of both endpoints).

activities.title: Address the Asset Discovery Problem
activities.do: Confront the asset discovery gap directly — you cannot scan a system you do not know exists — by going far beyond the CMDB across many data sources.
activities.output: Systems and assets register (integrated); Discovery gap register
activities.detail: Eleven asset discovery sources: (1) CMDB (often stale; validate/extend); (2) ITAM databases; (3) Procurement/purchasing records; (4) Cloud consoles/APIs (AWS Config, Azure Resource Graph, GCP Cloud Asset Inventory, CSPM — incl. non-production accounts); (5) Network scanning/traffic (Nmap, Shodan, NetFlow, DNS/DHCP logs — rogue/shadow IT/IoT); (6) Certificate Transparency logs; (7) DNS zone files/records; (8) Physical walkthroughs/site surveys (only reliable way for OT/embedded); (9) Service desk/incident records; (10) Third-party/vendor-managed systems; (11) M&A history. Decision Point: if the org cannot produce >80% IT / >60% OT asset coverage, it has a foundational problem to address; the quantum readiness program often becomes the forcing function for asset-inventory completeness.

activities.title: Integrate with Existing Data Sources
activities.do: Do not build the cryptographic inventory from scratch in isolation; integrate existing organizational data to save effort, improve accuracy, and inherit business context.
activities.output: Cryptographic asset inventory; Systems and assets register (integrated)
activities.detail: Integrate: CMDB (ownership, lifecycle, criticality, relationships); ITAM (hardware models, firmware, software licenses); Business Impact Assessments (criticality, RTO/RPO — flows into Phase 3 risk scoring); Data classification registers (feed HNDL scoring); Certificate Management Systems (inventory, expiry, issuer relationships, renewal history); SBOM (library versions, dependency trees, vulns); Vulnerability Management (crypto-library CVEs); CSPM (cloud encryption configs, KMS key policies); Network Security Monitoring (traffic flows, protocol negotiations); Enterprise Architecture repos; Procurement systems (vendor catalogs, contracts, licenses); Service catalogs/API registries; IAM systems (auth methods — cert-based, SAML/OIDC crypto deps); Backup/DR systems (encryption-at-rest configs, backup-encryption keys). The more sources integrated, the faster and more accurate the inventory.

activities.title: Establish Continuous Discovery
activities.do: Treat the cryptographic inventory as a living data set maintained continuously, spanning CI/CD integration, passive monitoring, change management, scheduled rescans, external intelligence, alerting, culture, and effectiveness metrics.
activities.detail: An inventory not continuously maintained decays within weeks; continuous discovery is also a prerequisite for crypto-agility. 1.6.1 CI/CD integration (SAST gates flag new quantum-vulnerable API calls; SCA dependency scanning; container/IaC scanning; CBOM auto-generation on deploy). 1.6.2 Passive network monitoring (taps/SPAN at DC borders, cloud transit, VPN concentrators, internet edge; baselines + deviation alerts). 1.6.3 Change management integration ('Cryptographic Impact' field on CAB templates; CBOM update as change-approval condition). 1.6.4 Scheduled rescans (Quarterly full network; Semi-annual deep; Annual comprehensive incl. physical OT walkthroughs; event-triggered after deployments/M&A/vuln disclosures). 1.6.5 External monitoring/intelligence (CT logs, EASM, crypto vuln intel cross-referenced to CBOM, standards/algorithm monitoring re-flagging entries for Phase 3 re-scoring). 1.6.6 Tiered alerting: Critical (deprecated/broken crypto in production, unknown internet-facing endpoint — remediate/isolate within 72h); High (quantum-vulnerable algorithm in new Tier-1 deploy — plan within 2 weeks); Medium (CBOM drift — within 1 month); Informational (log, next review). 1.6.7 Culture/training (train developers, designate crypto champions, feedback channels, inventory maintenance in objectives). 1.6.8 Effectiveness metrics: CBOM freshness ≥90% updated within 90 days; discovery-to-CBOM lag within 5 business days; drift rate <5%; unknown-unknowns closure −20%/quarter; time-to-detect new unauthorized endpoint within 7 days.

maturity_indicators.0: No cryptographic inventory exists; no awareness of the need
maturity_indicators.1: Partial manual inventory of obvious systems (web servers, VPN); CMDB-only asset register; no continuous discovery
maturity_indicators.2: Risk-driven scoping complete; automated discovery deployed on Priority A systems; ≥70% Tier-1 coverage; inventory is queryable; classical vulnerabilities being remediated; multiple asset data sources cross-referenced
maturity_indicators.3: ≥90% coverage; continuous discovery in CI/CD and passive monitoring; integrated with CMDB, SBOM, BIA, and certificate management; change management integration live; crypto champions designated; alerting framework operational
maturity_indicators.4: Real-time cryptographic posture monitoring with tiered alerting; automated drift detection; coverage spans IT, OT, cloud, and third-party; discovery effectiveness metrics tracked and reported; discovery gap register trending toward zero

common_failures.title: Interview-driven inventory
common_failures.why: Relying on application owners to self-report cryptographic usage; people don't know what crypto their systems use. Automated discovery supplemented by manual investigation is the only defensible approach.

common_failures.title: Spreadsheet-only inventory
common_failures.why: A static spreadsheet becomes stale within weeks; the inventory must be maintained in a queryable system with automated refresh.

common_failures.title: Waiting for 100% completeness before proceeding
common_failures.why: Completeness is asymptotic — you will never find everything. Use the 80/20 risk-driven scoping (Activity 1.0) to deliver actionable results quickly, proceed to Phase 2/3, and continue discovery in parallel.

common_failures.title: Ignoring OT and embedded systems
common_failures.why: These are often the hardest to discover AND the hardest to migrate; excluding them guarantees surprises later. Physical walkthroughs are essential for OT environments.

common_failures.title: Trusting a single tool for coverage
common_failures.why: No cryptographic discovery tool covers all five layers (network, code, config, runtime, manual). Deploy tools from multiple categories plus manual investigation.

common_failures.title: CMDB-only asset discovery
common_failures.why: The CMDB is rarely complete; relying solely on it undercounts the estate, particularly cloud resources, shadow IT, OT devices, and vendor-managed systems. Integrate the full range of data sources in Activity 1.4.

common_failures.title: Ignoring the immediate classical findings
common_failures.why: A quantum-focused inventory inevitably surfaces classically vulnerable cryptography; failing to remediate immediately wastes near-term security value and undermines the business case. Report and remediate classical findings in parallel.

common_failures.title: Treating discovery as a project with an end date
common_failures.why: Discovery is a permanent operational capability, not a phase that 'completes'. Organizations that disband the discovery team after the initial inventory find their CBOM becomes stale within 6 months.

gate.note: Phase 1 exit: risk-driven scoping document; cryptographic asset inventory (Priority A ≥90% within 60 days, ≥90% of all Tier-1 within 12 months); classical vulnerability findings reported; integrated sensitive-data map and systems/assets register; discovery gap register; continuous-discovery operating model.

phases.name: CBOM & Documentation
phases.summary: Transform raw Phase 1 inventory data into a durable, queryable, standardized Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) that serves as the single source of truth for all subsequent phases, making PQC migration auditable, plannable, and measurable.
phases.overlaps_with: Runs concurrently with Phase 1 (CBOM schema/tooling defined in the first weeks of Phase 1 so discovery data flows in structured) and with Phase 3 (ready CBOM entries, especially Layers 1–2, can be scored before full CBOM completion).

activities.title: Select CBOM Format and Tooling
activities.do: Choose the CBOM format and hosting platform and define the per-entry record structure. Recommended format is CycloneDX, the de facto CBOM standard with native support for cryptographic asset types (algorithms, certificates, keys, protocols, related dependencies).
activities.output: CycloneDX CBOM (format/tooling decision and record schema)
activities.detail: CycloneDX is supported by OWASP, adopted by the PQCC, and integrated into tooling from IBM, SandboxAQ, and the Linux Foundation's PQCA (CBOMkit). Each CBOM entry captures at minimum: Component identifier (links to asset inventory/CMDB); Algorithm OID; Key size / security parameter; Protocol context (TLS, IPsec, S/MIME); Implementation (library + version); Certificate reference; Data classification (from Track B of Phase 1); Quantum vulnerability status (Vulnerable (Shor), graded by quantum attack resource tier per algorithm and key size per Phase 3; weakened (Grover); safe); Migration status (Not started / Planned / In progress / Hybrid / PQC-only / Not applicable); Owner; Vendor dependency flag (self-controlled vs vendor-dependent).

activities.title: Populate CBOM from Inventory Data
activities.do: Map Phase 1 inventory data into CBOM records as a data transformation and enrichment exercise.
activities.detail: Six steps: 1) Import automated discovery results into CycloneDX using tool-native exporters or CBOMkit; 2) Enrich with manual investigation findings for systems not covered by automated tools; 3) Cross-reference with SBOM data to establish library dependency chains; 4) Link to certificate management system for PKI-related entries; 5) Add data classification tags from Track B of Phase 1; 6) Flag vendor dependencies from Track C of Phase 1.

activities.title: Integrate CBOM into Operational Processes
activities.do: Embed the CBOM into operational processes so it is a live system rather than a static document.
activities.detail: Integrate into: CI/CD pipelines (new deployments auto-generate/update CBOM entries; block deployments introducing quantum-vulnerable algorithms without documented justification and migration plan); Change management (CAB reviews include CBOM impact assessment); Vendor onboarding (new vendor products must provide CBOM-compatible cryptographic documentation as a procurement requirement); Audit and compliance (CBOM snapshots at regular intervals provide audit trail for regulatory evidence).

activities.title: Establish CBOM Freshness Governance
activities.do: Define trigger-to-action rules that keep the CBOM current.
activities.detail: Trigger/Action pairs: New system deployment → auto-generate CBOM entries via CI/CD; Library version update → update implementation version, check for algorithm changes; Certificate renewal/rotation → update certificate reference and validity dates; Quarterly full scan → reconcile CBOM against latest discovery results, flag discrepancies; Vendor product update → request updated CBOM data from vendor, update entries; Algorithm deprecation notice → flag all CBOM entries using deprecated algorithm, trigger Phase 3 re-scoring.

activities.title: Secure the CBOM and Program Artifacts
activities.do: Protect the CBOM, QRA, and prioritized migration backlog, which together form a map of every weak cryptographic point in the enterprise and a target-selection shopping list for HNDL adversaries.
activities.detail: Because the framework deliberately widens the CBOM's access surface (SIEM/SOC integration, GRC consumption, vendor CBOM exchange), protection is non-optional: Classify at the highest standard tier (typically Restricted); Apply role-based access with least privilege (broad dashboard access exposes aggregated posture metrics, not queryable system-level vulnerability detail); Log and review access (queries enumerating unmigrated systems get vulnerability-management-DB-level scrutiny); Control external sharing (vendors receive only entries relevant to their own products; auditors/regulators receive point-in-time extracts; consultant access ends with the engagement); Name CBOM exfiltration as a detection concern (the SOC's data exfiltration monitoring — SOC Use Case 5 — should include the CBOM repository and GRC evidence stores among high-sensitivity assets).

maturity_indicators.0: No CBOM exists; cryptographic documentation is ad hoc or absent
maturity_indicators.1: Partial CBOM in spreadsheet form covering known systems; no standard format
maturity_indicators.2: CycloneDX CBOM operational for Layers 1–2; queryable; SBOM linkage established for key applications
maturity_indicators.3: CBOM covers Layers 1–3; integrated into CI/CD; freshness governance enforced; change management integration live
maturity_indicators.4: CBOM is a real-time operational asset; auto-updated on deployment; Layer 4 gaps systematically managed through vendor governance; CBOM drives automated compliance reporting

common_failures.title: Completeness trap
common_failures.why: Insisting on 100% CBOM coverage before proceeding to risk scoring and migration. Layer 4 (embedded/third-party) will never be fully visible — accept this, document the gaps, and manage through vendor governance.

common_failures.title: CBOM as document, not system
common_failures.why: Producing a CBOM in a PDF or spreadsheet that is never updated. The CBOM must be a live, queryable data set integrated into operational processes.

common_failures.title: Ignoring the SBOM-CBOM linkage
common_failures.why: CBOM entries without SBOM context miss critical dependency chains; a vulnerable algorithm in a widely-shared library affects every application that depends on it.

gate.note: Phase 2 exit (CycloneDX CBOM operational for Layers 1–2 with freshness governance and protection controls) corresponds to the G2->G3 transition; authoritative gate criteria live in the global stage_gates table.

phases.name: Risk Scoring & Prioritization
phases.summary: Translate CBOM data into a defensible, sequenced migration priority list, producing the prioritized backlog and Quantum Readiness Assessment (QRA) that drive Phase 4 roadmap planning and Phase 5 execution sequencing. A structured, transparent scoring model depoliticizes sequencing by replacing opinion with repeatable criteria.
phases.overlaps_with: Runs in parallel with Phase 2 (begins as soon as CBOM entries are sufficiently enriched, scoring Layers 1–2 while Layer 3 discovery continues) and with itself iteratively — the QRA is a living document re-run at least quarterly as inventory, regulatory deadlines, vendor timelines, and NIST standards evolve.

activities.title: Define Risk Scoring Model
activities.do: Define a quantum-specific risk scoring model that extends established information security risk methodologies (ISO/IEC 27005, NIST SP 800-30, NIST RMF). Default weights are a starting configuration to be calibrated by sector, risk profile, and regulatory context. Score each CBOM entry across four dimensions.
activities.detail: Dimension 1 — Data Sensitivity × Exposure Window (HNDL Risk): Data confidentiality requirement in years (High weight; >15yr=Critical, 10–15yr=High, 5–10yr=Medium, <5yr=Low); Data volume/flow rate (Medium); Accessibility to adversary (High; Internet-facing=Critical, Partner-facing=High, Internal=Medium, Air-gapped=Low). Dimension 2 — Trust Infrastructure Criticality (TNFL Risk): Key/certificate lifetime (High; Root CA (20yr)=Critical, Intermediate CA (10yr)=High, End-entity (1yr)=Medium); Scope of trust dependency (High); Signature verification period (Medium; Firmware signed 15yr=Critical). Dimension 3 — Migration Feasibility: Control posture (High; Full control=Easy, Vendor-dependent=Hard); Protocol/standard maturity (Medium); Interoperability constraints (Medium); System age and architecture (Medium). Dimension 4 — Regulatory and Compliance Pressure: Specific regulatory deadline (High; within 2 years=Critical); Audit exposure (Medium); Contractual requirement (Medium). Algorithm-Specific Vulnerability Weighting: quantum attack cost scales with key size, not classical strength; at equal classical security P-256 vs RSA-3072, breaking the ECC key needs ~2.6× fewer logical qubits and two orders of magnitude fewer Toffoli gates; treat ECC-256 and RSA-2048 as the same urgency tier, with RSA-3072+ one tier behind; do not deprioritize ECC-protected assets; record algorithm + key size in each CBOM entry so the weighting is applied mechanically.

activities.title: Calculate Priority Scores
activities.do: Compute a composite priority score for each CBOM entry and classify it into a migration urgency tier.
activities.detail: Priority = (HNDL Risk × 0.35) + (TNFL Risk × 0.25) + (Regulatory Pressure × 0.25) + (Migration Feasibility Inverse × 0.15). Feasibility is inverted because harder migrations may need earlier starts (longer lead times) despite lower risk; weighting reflects HNDL as the most immediately exploitable threat. Urgency tiers: Tier 1 Immediate (Critical HNDL + high accessibility + feasible; begin within 6 months, hybrid within 12); Tier 2 High Priority (High HNDL/TNFL + regulatory deadline within 3 years; begin within 12 months, hybrid within 24); Tier 3 Standard (Medium risk + feasible with vendor coordination; begin within 24 months, complete within regulatory deadline); Tier 4 Long Tail (Lower risk OR currently infeasible; monitor, compensating controls, migrate when feasible).

activities.title: Apply Migration Sequencing Logic
activities.do: Sequence the prioritized backlog within the Two-Track Migration Model from Phase 5: Track A (key exchange and confidentiality) and Track B (signatures, PKI, authentication) run as parallel workstreams, not a serial list. v2.1 retires the earlier key-exchange-then-signatures-then-data-at-rest serialization because treating signatures as second systematically delays the migrations with the longest lead times.
activities.detail: Within each tier: 1) Track A — key exchange (TLS, VPN, key establishment), sequenced by exposure: internet-facing TLS and partner VPNs first (each migrated channel immediately stops creating new HNDL-vulnerable sessions), then internal east-west, then app-embedded key establishment. 2) Track B — signatures and PKI (code/firmware signing, CA infrastructure, document signing), sequenced by trust-anchor longevity and lead time: code and firmware signing first (a forged update cascades through every downstream system — SolarWinds pattern without the months of infiltration), then CA modernization and key-lifetime reduction, then end-entity/document signing; TNFL exploitation requires an operational CRQC, but signature migration has the longest lead times (PKI architecture, toolchain, HSM dependencies), which is why Track B starts in parallel. 3) Data at rest (within Track A): re-encrypt long-lived archives with AES-256 or apply PQC-aware key wrapping (Activity 5.5); lower urgency than data in transit, but stores with the longest confidentiality horizons must not fall off the roadmap.

activities.title: Produce the Quantum Readiness Assessment (QRA)
activities.do: Consolidate risk scoring into a formal Quantum Readiness Assessment document as the defensible basis for migration planning and regulatory evidence.
activities.detail: QRA contents: Executive summary (overall quantum risk posture; aggregate maturity score; comparison to regulatory deadlines); Heatmap (risk across the estate by system tier and domain); Prioritized migration backlog (sequenced list of all CBOM entries with tier assignments, target timelines, owner assignments); Gap analysis (where posture falls short of regulatory requirements, with remediation actions); Compliance mapping (QRA outputs mapped to NIST, CNSA 2.0, ETSI, and sector-specific requirements).

maturity_indicators.1: Informal awareness of which systems are "probably vulnerable"; no structured scoring
maturity_indicators.2: Formal risk scoring model applied to Tier-1 CBOM entries; prioritized migration backlog exists; QRA document produced
maturity_indicators.3: QRA updated quarterly; all CBOM entries scored and tiered; migration sequencing drives Phase 5 execution; legal risk dimension assessed
maturity_indicators.4: Continuous risk posture management; automated re-scoring when CBOM changes or regulatory deadlines shift; QRA integrated into enterprise risk register and audit cycle

common_failures.title: Equal priority for everything
common_failures.why: Treating all quantum-vulnerable crypto as equally urgent, which dilutes resources and yields no meaningful progress on the highest-risk systems.

common_failures.title: Ignoring migration feasibility in prioritization
common_failures.why: Assigning highest priority to systems that cannot be migrated yet (no vendor support, no standard) while ignoring high-risk systems that could be migrated today.

common_failures.title: Static risk assessment
common_failures.why: Producing the QRA once and never updating it; risk scores change as standards mature, vendor products ship, and regulatory deadlines approach.

common_failures.title: Neglecting the legal and data-retention dimension
common_failures.why: Organizations storing long-lived encrypted data face compounding legal risk — data encrypted today with quantum-vulnerable algorithms may become decryptable later, potentially violating data-protection principles (e.g. GDPR security requirements) and contractual confidentiality. The QRA should prompt a legal risk assessment alongside the technical one; engage legal counsel early.

common_failures.title: Assuming ECC's classical strength buys quantum time
common_failures.why: Migrating RSA first because it is classically weaker misreads the threat model; quantum attack cost tracks key size, so 256-bit ECC keys are at least as exposed as RSA-2048 and more exposed than RSA-3072. Apply the algorithm-specific weighting in Activity 3.1.

gate.note: Phase 3 exit (scored/tiered CBOM and a produced QRA with prioritized backlog ready for Phase 4) corresponds to the G3->G4 transition; authoritative gate criteria live in the global stage_gates table.

phases.name: Phase 4 — Roadmap & Governance
phases.cadence: continuous (living instrument; initial roadmap drafted as soon as first Phase 3 risk scoring outputs are available, revised quarterly thereafter)
phases.summary: Translate the prioritized Phase 3 migration backlog into a multi-year execution plan with realistic milestones, resource allocations, vendor coordination timelines, and governance checkpoints. Establishes PMO discipline and models external constraints (vendor GA dates, hardware refresh, regulatory deadlines, scarce crypto skills) explicitly, not just internal work sequencing.
phases.overlaps_with: Runs in parallel with Phases 5, 6, and 7 (roadmap is a living instrument revised quarterly); activates Phase 7 vendor engagement immediately; Phases 1 and 2 discovery/CBOM continue throughout

activities.title: Define Year-1 Starter Plan (90-Day Governance Sprint)
activities.do: Deliver five things in the first 90 days across Organization, People, Plan, Policy/Procurement, and KPI pack; then execute a quarter-by-quarter Year-1 detailed plan (Q1-Q4) spanning Governance & People, Discovery & CBOM, Pilots & Technical, and Vendor & Policy workstreams.
activities.detail: Five deliverables: (1) Organization — executive sponsor and QRPM confirmed; SteerCo calendar and charter published; RACI matrix for all workstreams. (2) People — 10-to-20 person training cohort enrolled in PQC fundamentals; crypto champions designated per platform team. (3) Plan — Crypto-BOM v1 with >=70% Tier-1 coverage; 2 hybrid pilots selected (TLS and VPN); vendor questionnaires sent to top 10 strategic vendors. (4) Policy/Procurement — cryptographic policy updated (approved cipher suites include PQC hybrids; shorter key lifetimes for new certificates); PQC and crypto-agility clause added to all new RFPs and contract renewals. (5) KPI pack — baseline values established; Q+1 targets set; board reporting template ready. Quarterly plan: Q1 appoint QRPM/SteerCo/charter/RACI, deploy Priority A discovery on internet-facing Tier-1, begin CBOM structure design, select 2 pilot targets, set up lab/staging, send questionnaires to top 10 vendors; Q2 first SteerCo milestone review, complete Priority A and begin Priority B discovery, publish Crypto-BOM v1 (>=70% Tier-1), execute pilots in lab/staging and measure baselines, classify vendors by PQC criticality; Q3 present QRA findings, refine Year 2 budget, begin Phase 3 risk scoring on Priority A, integrate CBOM into CI/CD, promote validated pilots to production canary (1-5% traffic), begin Wave 1 planning, follow up non-responsive vendors and insert PQC clauses into renewals; Q4 first formal quarterly board report, complete QRA for Tier-1, publish Crypto-BOM v2 (>=90% Tier-1, >=60% Tier-2), establish continuous discovery rhythm, complete canary validation and begin Wave 2, publish vendor PQC scorecard, set Year 2 vendor engagement calendar, finalize multi-year roadmap.

activities.title: Structure the Multi-Year Roadmap
activities.do: Lay out a 5-year roadmap with a focus theme and key milestones per year.
activities.detail: Year 1 Foundation — Crypto-BOM v1; 2-4 hybrid pilots (TLS, VPN); vendor commitments secured; policy updates; team training. Year 2 Tier-1 Rollout — hybrid/PQC deployed on all Tier-1 internet-facing endpoints; PKI key-lifetime reductions; dual-sign pilots for code signing. Year 3 Bulk Migration — Tier-2 systems migrated; internal east-west traffic hybrid-enabled; HSM firmware upgrades; vendor product upgrades tracked. Year 4 Long Tail & OT — Tier-3/4 systems; OT gateway protections; embedded device migration or containment; compensating controls where infeasible. Year 5 Hardening & Agility — eliminate remaining compensating controls; achieve crypto-agility across the estate; transition hybrid to PQC-only where ecosystem supports; achieve target maturity level.

activities.title: Align to Infrastructure Refresh Cycles
activities.do: Map migration tasks to existing planned expenditures so PQC piggybacks on already-funded infrastructure changes.
activities.detail: Refresh-to-opportunity mapping: Data center network refresh -> PQC-capable switches/load balancers, hybrid TLS at edge; SD-WAN/VPN upgrade -> require PQC support in new concentrators, hybrid IPsec; Cloud migration wave -> PQC-capable TLS on cloud load balancers, cloud-native PQC KMS; PKI renewal/CA migration -> PQC-capable CA, hybrid/composite certs, shorter lifetimes; HSM replacement cycle -> procure PQC-capable HSMs (Thales Luna v7.9+, Utimaco Quantum Protect, or equivalent); Vendor contract renewal -> insert PQC roadmap requirements, crypto-agility clauses, SLAs; Application modernization -> cryptographic abstraction layers, replace hardcoded algorithm calls with provider pattern.

activities.title: Establish PMO Structure for Scale
activities.do: For programs exceeding 10,000 tasks, stand up PMO machinery and map/track the critical dependency chains.
activities.detail: Establish: WBS aligned to the 8 workstreams from Phase 0; dependency mapping between workstreams; critical path analysis (longest dependency chain determines minimum program duration); resource leveling to avoid overloading shared teams (PKI, security architecture, vendor management); risk register with escalation triggers (e.g. 'if vendor X misses PQC GA date by >6 months, escalate to SteerCo for alternate vendor'). Critical dependency chains: CBOM v1 before risk scoring; risk scoring before pilot target selection; HSM firmware upgrade before HSM-dependent app migration; PKI CA modernization before dual-sign/PQC certificate deployment; library upgrade before application hybrid enablement; vendor PQC GA release before migration of vendor-dependent systems; network middlebox testing before production hybrid deployment on affected paths; procurement policy update before new system acquisitions. Typical critical path: Discovery -> CBOM -> Risk Scoring -> Roadmap -> Pilot -> Production Rollout, with vendor engagement in parallel from Q1 Year 1 and vendor GA gating pilot/rollout (vendor dependency usually the longest segment).

activities.title: Manage the Roadmap as a Living Instrument
activities.do: Treat the roadmap as a living instrument, not a static Gantt chart; run a quarterly roadmap review as a standing SteerCo agenda item presenting KPIs alongside leading indicators, and apply a decision playbook when adjustment is needed.
activities.detail: Leading indicators reviewed quarterly: Quantum technology signals (logical qubit milestones, resource-estimate drops, gate speed, lab announcements); Adversary signals (HNDL campaign intel, supply-chain targeting of PKI/code-signing toolchains); Standards/regulatory signals (NIST/IETF/ETSI/ISO updates, parameter changes, hybrid profiles to RFCs, new/earlier mandates); Vendor milestone signals (GA dates met/missed, new PQC products, FIPS validation completions). Decision playbook: KPIs off track -> add resources, descope lower-risk items, pull forward bridging patterns; leading indicators worsen (CRQC timeline shortens) -> move to accelerated track with pre-drafted resource request; performance issues at scale -> deploy offload/scale-out, adjust SLOs, extend pilot windows; critical vendor misses a date -> activate champion-challenger (Phase 7), deploy bridging pattern, escalate contractually.

activities.title: Define Milestone Gates
activities.do: Define a milestone gate review for each phase transition, with explicit criteria and a decision authority per gate.
activities.detail: Phase 4's own exit gate is G3 -> G4: 'Multi-year roadmap approved; Year 1 plan resourced' with Decision Authority = Executive Sponsor. (The full G0->G7 transition table is in stage_gates.)

activities.title: Pre-Draft the Accelerated Execution Profile
activities.do: Pre-draft the accelerated track as a concrete, pre-approved artifact before it is needed, and exercise it annually as a tabletop scenario.
activities.detail: Pre-approved package with five elements: (1) trigger conditions — a credible reassessment of CRQC timelines by a SteerCo-designated source, regulatory deadline compression, or a cryptanalytic event against a deployed algorithm; (2) compressed sequence — discovery narrows to Priority A, the CBOM accepts documented Layer 3/4 gaps, Waves 2–4 merge into a single accelerated rollout with relaxed canary thresholds, lower-tier systems move directly to compensating controls (segmentation, overlay encryption, key-lifetime reduction) rather than full migration; (3) pre-approved risk acceptances signed in advance so invocation does not wait on committee cycles; (4) pre-drafted resource request — contractor capacity identified, emergency procurement clauses pre-negotiated, pre-authorized budget reallocation; (5) activation authority — who can invoke and through which escalation path. Exercise the profile annually as a tabletop (the SOC Implementation foundation provides the exercise structure).

maturity_indicators.1: Informal plan exists (spreadsheet, no governance); single-year horizon
maturity_indicators.2: Multi-year roadmap approved; Year 1 plan resourced; SteerCo operational; KPI baseline set
maturity_indicators.3: Quarterly roadmap reviews operational; dependency mapping maintained; refresh cycle alignment documented; vendor engagement tracked on dashboard
maturity_indicators.4: Roadmap is a living instrument with quarterly updates; contingency triggers defined and tested; leading indicators monitored; program transitioning from migration execution to ongoing posture management

common_failures.title: Planning in isolation from refresh cycles.
common_failures.why: Building a PQC migration plan that ignores existing hardware refresh, cloud migration, and vendor contract renewal schedules, resulting in 'big-bang' budget requests that get rejected and missed opportunities to embed PQC into already-funded programs.

common_failures.title: Underestimating the vendor dependency on the critical path.
common_failures.why: The longest segment of most PQC migration critical paths is waiting for vendor products to ship PQC support; organizations that start vendor engagement in Year 2 instead of Q1 Year 1 discover too late that their timeline is vendor-constrained and cannot be compressed with internal effort alone.

common_failures.title: Single-track roadmap with no contingencies.
common_failures.why: A roadmap that assumes every vendor delivers on time, every pilot succeeds first try, and no regulatory timeline changes; build in explicit contingency triggers and pre-drafted acceleration/deceleration plans.

common_failures.title: Treating the roadmap as a project plan rather than a program plan.
common_failures.why: PQC migration is not a project with a defined end date but a permanent operational capability (crypto-agility); the roadmap should transition from 'migration execution' to 'ongoing cryptographic posture management' by Year 4-5, not declare victory and disband the team.

common_failures.title: Governance without teeth.
common_failures.why: Establishing a SteerCo that meets but does not make binding decisions, approve funding, or hold workstream leads accountable; the governance structure must have decision authority over budget, timelines, risk acceptance, and vendor escalation.

gate.note: Phase 4 exit corresponds to gate G3 -> G4: 'Multi-year roadmap approved; Year 1 plan resourced' (Executive Sponsor), per Activity 4.6's milestone gate table at lines ~3932-3933

phases.name: Phase 5 — Pilots & Migration Execution
phases.cadence: iterative (controlled pilots validated then scaled to production through sequential waves Wave 0-5)
phases.summary: Execute the migration through controlled pilots, validate patterns, and scale to production through waves, operationalizing the Phase 4 roadmap starting with the highest-priority, most-controllable systems. Produces the program's first tangible security outcomes and deliberately surfaces infrastructure incompatibilities, performance regressions, middlebox failures, and interoperability problems in a controlled setting with tested rollback.
phases.overlaps_with: Runs concurrently with Phase 6 (Infrastructure Modernization) and Phase 7 (Vendor Governance) in a tightly coupled feedback loop; Phase 1 discovery and Phase 2 CBOM maintenance continue throughout

activities.title: Select Pilot Targets
activities.do: Choose 2-4 initial pilots based on Tier-1 priority from Phase 3 risk scoring, full organizational control of both endpoints, a measurable baseline, representative architecture, and rollback capability.
activities.output: Pilot results reports (pilot candidates for both Track A and Track B)
activities.detail: Selection criteria: Tier-1 priority; full organizational control (both endpoints, no external partner dependency); measurable baseline; representative architecture; rollback capability. Recommended starter pilots: Hybrid TLS on internet-facing web app (highest HNDL exposure, strong library/browser support — proves PQC key exchange at scale); Hybrid IPsec/VPN between two controlled sites (proves PQC for site-to-site, validates concentrator/firewall compatibility); Internal mTLS between microservices (east-west, high-volume — proves service mesh PQC capability, library compatibility); Certificate lifecycle with shortened validity (proves PKI can handle increased rotation frequency).

activities.title: Design Hybrid Deployments
activities.do: Default to Hybrid ML-KEM-768 + X25519 for TLS key exchange (the X25519MLKEM768 named group in TLS 1.3); choose hybrid over pure PQC for the stated reasons; default to composite/dual signatures where toolchains support them; and verify cryptographic library readiness before committing to a deployment pattern.
activities.detail: NIST SP 800-227 discusses the related X-Wing hybrid KEM. Why hybrid not pure PQC: (1) immediate quantum resistance without waiting for universal PQC adoption; (2) preserves interoperability during phased rollout when support exists (test, don't assume); (3) reduces deployment risk (protected against known quantum threats and unknown weaknesses in new PQC algorithms); (4) proven at large production scale (Chrome/Chromium, Cloudflare, AWS; Cloudflare reports a majority of human-generated TLS traffic now uses PQC-hybrid key exchange). Hybrid signatures (framework position): composite/dual signatures (classical + PQC) the default wherever toolchains support; published analysis of early ML-DSA implementation flaws (Bernstein, June 2026) estimates dropping the classical layer increases breakable signature keys by ~an order of magnitude over five years; deploying solo ML-DSA is a recorded risk decision, not a default. Per-protocol architecture: TLS 1.3 (X25519 + ML-KEM-768 / X-Wing SP 800-227; production-ready); IPsec IKEv2 (ECDH P-256 + ML-KEM-768; RFC 9370); SSH (X25519 + ML-KEM-768; OpenSSH 9.9+ mlkem768x25519-sha256, default from 10.0); S/MIME (ECDH P-256 + ML-KEM-768; IETF drafts, limited); Code Signing (ECDSA P-256 + ML-DSA-65; composite IETF, early); FIDO2/WebAuthn (ES256/RS256 + ML-DSA; COSE PQC identifiers IANA Apr 2025; not yet); Token signing JWT/OIDC/SAML (RS256/ES256 + ML-DSA; JOSE/COSE drafts, early). Library readiness: OpenSSL native ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA since 3.5 (Apr 2025); BoringSSL/Chrome (ML-KEM Sep 2024, default Chrome 131); AWS-LC (first open-source FIPS 140-3 validated with ML-KEM); Bouncy Castle (Java); wolfSSL (embedded/IoT, CNSA 2.0 aligned); Libsodium/MbedTLS (limited/in progress). If a library lacks PQC: upgrade, switch library, or deploy a PQC-capable gateway/proxy bridge. Hybrid mandate divergence: BSI/ANSSI/Netherlands strongly recommend or require hybrid; NCSC UK prefers single migration to pure PQC but accepts hybrid as interim; NIST permits not requires; NSA CNSA 2.0 accepts hybrid as interim only. Multinational recommendation: adopt hybrid as default interim bridge to PQC-only.

activities.title: Execute Pilots with Measurement
activities.do: For each pilot, define and measure performance SLOs, anticipate expected performance impacts, and define explicit rollback criteria/triggers.
activities.output: Pilot results reports (performance data, compatibility findings, issues log, recommendations)
activities.detail: Performance SLOs: handshake latency (p50/p95/p99 before/after); CPU utilization (server + client delta); connection throughput; error rates (connection failures, negotiation fallbacks, compatibility); memory utilization. Expected impacts: TLS 1.3 hybrid (e.g. X25519MLKEM768) — materially larger ClientHello and ~1 KB additional key-exchange data per handshake; real latency impact path-, MTU-, middlebox-dependent (a measurement exercise); ML-KEM CPU typically negligible on modern hardware, dominant factor is packetization and middlebox behavior. IPsec hybrid — similar latency, slightly higher CPU. Signature verification (ML-DSA) — ML-DSA-44 ~2,420 bytes, ML-DSA-65 ~3,309 bytes vs ~64 bytes for ECDSA P-256 (where real infrastructure stress appears). Rollback triggers: error rate exceeds X% above baseline; latency p99 exceeds Y ms above baseline; security vulnerability in PQC implementation; interoperability failure with a critical downstream system.

activities.title: Scale from Pilot to Production Through Waves
activities.do: Sequence deployment through controlled waves, each with a defined scope and an explicit prerequisite gate from the prior wave.
activities.detail: Wave 0 Lab/Staging (isolated test; prerequisite: pilot design approved); Wave 1 Internal Non-Critical (dev tools, monitoring, non-critical APIs; prerequisite: lab validation passed); Wave 2 Internal Production (internal Tier-1, east-west; prerequisite: Wave 1 metrics acceptable); Wave 3 External Controlled (partner-facing APIs with cooperative counterparties; prerequisite: Wave 2 stable, partner coordination complete); Wave 4 External Broad (public-facing web apps, customer APIs; prerequisite: Wave 3 stable, external compatibility validated); Wave 5 Long Tail (legacy, OT gateways, embedded; prerequisite: vendor support available or containment strategy deployed).

activities.title: Implement Defense-in-Depth Beyond Pure PQC
activities.do: Complement hybrid/PQC deployment with layered controls that reduce cryptographic protection surface and protect data across in-transit, at-rest, and in-use states.
activities.detail: Tokenization (replace sensitive data with tokens — a scope reducer eliminating categories of HNDL exposure); data minimization and retention reduction (delete data with no business value); network segmentation (isolate high-value data flows into enhanced-monitoring zones); AES-256 as universal symmetric default (Grover-resistant; low-effort high-impact vs AES-128); key lifetime reduction (a 90-day certificate limits the TNFL window vs a 2-year cert); Confidential Computing as complementary (hardware TEEs protect data in use — PQC in transit, AES-256 at rest, Confidential Computing during processing; Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, ARM CCA); enhanced key wrapping for data at rest (wrap existing DEKs with PQC key encapsulation rather than re-encrypting petabyte-scale archives).

activities.title: Decide the Data-at-Rest Strategy
activities.do: Make a per-data-store choice among five data-at-rest strategies, driven by the data's confidentiality horizon (Phase 1 classification), volume, and exfiltration exposure; record the chosen strategy per data store in the CBOM.
activities.output: Per-data-store strategy recorded in the CBOM
activities.detail: Data at rest is sequenced after data in transit (3.3) since an adversary must exfiltrate stored ciphertext before HNDL applies. Five strategies: Re-encrypt under PQC-protected keys (high-sensitivity, long-horizon data in actively managed stores; watch throughput/downtime, verify no copy under old keys survives); PQC key-wrap (KEK/DEK redesign) (large stores where re-encrypting data is infeasible; protects keys not already-exfiltrated ciphertext, requires KMS/HSM PQC support); Crypto-shred (destroy the keys) (data past its confidentiality requirement that policy cannot yet delete; produce destruction evidence per the closure standard); Delete (no remaining business/legal value; requires legal sign-off); Accept and monitor (low-sensitivity/short-horizon; a recorded risk decision with a re-evaluation trigger, not a default). Backups/archives: tape libraries and immutable backups cannot be re-encrypted in place — let old generations age out under a documented schedule while new generations write under PQC-protected keys, with key-wrap on long-retention archives; petabyte-scale decrypt-old/re-encrypt-new is a Phase 6 capacity exercise.

activities.title: AI-Assisted Migration: Where It Helps, and the Gate That Stays Closed
activities.do: Use AI tooling where it genuinely accelerates migration (triage and drafting) while holding a non-negotiable gate that AI-modified cryptographic code passes the same (or more) review/testing/validation rigor as human-written code; keep algorithm selection, parameter choices, and risk acceptances as human decisions, and record AI-assisted provenance.
activities.output: AI-assisted provenance recorded on migrated components
activities.detail: Where AI genuinely accelerates: triaging discovery findings at Layer 3 scale; enriching CBOM entries from vendor documentation; generating test cases and interoperability matrices; drafting repetitive engineering artifacts (configuration variants, rollout runbooks). Fine-tuned models demonstrated ~92% functional correctness on cryptographic code migration in 2026 research — argues for using the tooling on triage and drafting, not for trusting the output (at estate scale remaining failures land somewhere, and a functional-looking failure in cryptographic code can be a security failure). The non-negotiable gate: AI-modified cryptographic code passes the same review, testing, and validation rigor as human-written code, and where the change touches key generation, signing, or protocol state machines, more rigor not less. Algorithm selection, parameter choices, and risk acceptances remain human decisions; record AI-assisted provenance so reviewers and auditors know which artifacts carry it. The failure mode to refuse: treating AI throughput as a reason to compress review; the tooling buys speed in the steps before and after review, never in review itself.

maturity_indicators.0: No PQC pilots planned or underway
maturity_indicators.1: Lab testing only; no production exposure
maturity_indicators.2: 2+ production pilots running with measured results; rollback procedures tested; validated patterns documented
maturity_indicators.3: Tier-1 internet-facing systems on hybrid/PQC; wave rollout underway for Tier-2; defense-in-depth measures (tokenization, AES-256, segmentation) deployed
maturity_indicators.4: Estate-wide hybrid/PQC deployment substantially complete; transitioning selected systems from hybrid to PQC-only; crypto-agility demonstrated via algorithm-swap drill

common_failures.title: Piloting the easy systems, not the important ones.
common_failures.why: Choosing pilot targets by convenience rather than Phase 3 risk prioritization; a pilot that succeeds on a developer sandbox proves little — pilots must prove PQC works on the highest-priority, highest-risk systems.

common_failures.title: Skipping rollback planning.
common_failures.why: Deploying hybrid/PQC without a tested, documented rollback path; when a pilot causes unexpected failures, the team must revert within minutes, not hours — define rollback triggers and test the procedure before going live.

common_failures.title: 'Big bang' instead of waves.
common_failures.why: Attempting to migrate all Tier-1 systems simultaneously rather than sequencing through controlled waves (lab -> internal non-critical -> internal production -> external controlled -> external broad -> long tail), where each wave validates assumptions and generates lessons for the next.

common_failures.title: Ignoring library version as a hard constraint.
common_failures.why: Designing a pilot for a system whose cryptographic library does not yet support PQC; verify library readiness (5.2) before committing, otherwise the pilot becomes a library upgrade project with different risks and timelines.

common_failures.title: Measuring only latency, ignoring compatibility.
common_failures.why: Focusing pilot metrics on handshake latency while neglecting compatibility with downstream systems, middleboxes, monitoring tools, and partner endpoints — the most common production failures from PQC deployment are compatibility issues, not performance.

common_failures.title: Treating hybrid as the end state.
common_failures.why: Hybrid is a transition mechanism, not a permanent architecture; organizations that deploy hybrid and declare victory face a second migration when hybrid is deprecated or when jurisdictions (NCSC UK, CNSA 2.0) require pure PQC — plan the hybrid-to-PQC-only transition from the start.

gate.note: Phase 5 exit corresponds to gate G5 -> G6: 'Pilots validated; performance baselines established; Tier-1 rollout approved' (SteerCo)

phases.name: Infrastructure Modernization & Performance
phases.summary: Modernize the cryptographic infrastructure stack (PKI, HSMs, KMS, network devices, middleboxes) to support PQC operations at production scale, and address the performance, capacity, and compatibility challenges PQC introduces to real infrastructure.
phases.overlaps_with: Runs iteratively alongside Phase 5 (pilots reveal infra issues; infra upgrades enable broader pilots — a continuous feedback loop); depends heavily on Phase 7 vendor timelines. Early-start activities (HSM inventory, PKI lifetime reduction) begin as early as Phase 0/1.

activities.title: PKI Modernization
activities.do: Address PQC's fundamental challenges to PKI (certificate size explosion, increased chain verification time, middlebox compatibility) by executing the PKI migration strategy: shorten key lifetimes immediately, deploy dual-stack CA infrastructure, track Merkle Tree Certificates for web PKI, and test certificate chain processing through all middleboxes before production.
activities.detail: Certificate size explosion: ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes (ML-DSA-44 is 2,420 bytes) versus ~64 bytes for ECDSA. Strategy steps: (1) Shorten key lifetimes immediately — root CA from 20+ years to 10 years, intermediate CAs to 5 years, end-entity to 90–365 days (limits TNFL exposure, builds rotation muscle). (2) Deploy dual-stack CA infrastructure — PQC-capable CA alongside classical CA; issue hybrid/composite certificates; maintain classical-only certs for systems not ready. (3) Track Merkle Tree Certificates (MTC) for web PKI — Google/Cloudflare MTC initiative live-testing in Chrome as of early 2026 under IETF PLANTS WG; CA signs a Merkle tree head, browser gets a compact inclusion proof (<1 KB); still experimental, not yet a near-term compliance obligation. (4) Test certificate chain processing — verify all middleboxes (firewalls, WAFs, IDS/IPS, DLP, forward proxies) process PQC chains without failure or truncation before any production deployment.

activities.title: HSM and KMS Modernization
activities.do: Inventory all HSMs by model, firmware version, and PQC capability (immediate); upgrade HSM firmware to PQC-capable versions as available; plan HSM hardware replacement aligned to refresh cycle where firmware upgrade is insufficient; configure cloud KMS for PQC key types as available; and deploy software-based PQC key-wrapping overlay as a bridge for HSMs not yet upgradeable.
activities.detail: Many HSMs in production cannot support PQC without firmware or hardware upgrade. Thales Luna 7.8.0+ introduced initial PQC support (ML-KEM, ML-DSA); Luna 7.9 (June 2025) adds further PQC capabilities. Utimaco Quantum Protect is a new hardware variant (not a firmware upgrade for existing devices — budget for hardware replacement if running older Utimaco models). Budget for a 2–4 year replacement cycle where hardware replacement is needed. Cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS): check current PQC support status. As a bridge, use PQC key-wrapping around classical HSM operations for interim protection.

activities.title: Network Infrastructure Assessment
activities.do: Test the ways PQC impacts network infrastructure before production deployment, covering handshake size impact and protocol-specific concerns (TLS 1.3, DTLS/UDP, IKEv2/IPsec, QUIC, constrained IoT, satellite/LPWAN, mobile networks), applying the per-protocol mitigations.
activities.detail: Handshake size impact: classical TLS 1.3 ~1–2 KB; hybrid TLS 1.3 (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) ~2–3 KB (key exchange adds ~1 KB); PQC certificate chain with ML-DSA can exceed 10 KB for a 3-certificate chain. Protocol concerns/mitigations: TLS 1.3 — larger ClientHello may fragment, some middleboxes reject oversized handshakes → test with production middleboxes, verify MTU handling, consider TLS certificate compression. DTLS (UDP) — larger handshake fragments, amplification concerns → test fragmentation handling, verify anti-amplification mechanisms. IKEv2/IPsec — larger IKE_SA_INIT messages, fragmentation across VPN concentrators → use IKE fragmentation (RFC 7383), test with production VPN devices. QUIC — designed for larger handshakes, generally more PQC-friendly → test with production load balancers. Constrained IoT (CoAP, LPWAN) — extremely limited bandwidth, PQC key sizes may be prohibitive → consider pre-shared key approaches, gateway-based PQC termination, sector-specific protocols. Satellite/LPWAN — high latency and limited bandwidth exacerbate handshake size impact → use session resumption aggressively, consider PQC gateway at ground station. Mobile networks — handshake latency affects UX, cellular bandwidth constraints → test on representative cellular connections, measure impact on connection establishment time.

activities.title: Performance Testing Methodology
activities.do: For each system targeted for PQC migration, execute baseline measurement, lab validation, canary deployment, SLO evaluation, and capacity planning.
activities.detail: (1) Baseline measurement: capture current performance metrics (latency p50/p95/p99, CPU utilization, memory, throughput) under representative production load. (2) Lab validation: deploy hybrid/PQC in isolated test environment; measure same metrics. (3) Canary deployment: deploy to 1–5% of production traffic with A/B comparison. (4) SLO evaluation: compare canary metrics against SLOs defined in Phase 5. (5) Capacity planning: if PQC requires additional compute/memory/bandwidth, estimate requirements for full production rollout and include in Phase 4 budget.

activities.title: Capacity Planning for PQC at Scale
activities.do: Plan for the expected resource impact of PQC across CPU, memory, network bandwidth, and storage, taking the prescribed planning action for each.
activities.output: Performance baseline and projections (capacity plan for production rollout)
activities.detail: CPU — ML-KEM key generation/encapsulation: minimal impact; ML-DSA signature verification: moderate → benchmark on production hardware, plan for 5–15% server CPU increase for signature-heavy workloads. Memory — larger key material and expanded TLS session state → minimal for most systems, test on memory-constrained devices. Network bandwidth — hybrid handshakes add ~1 KB; PQC certificates add 2–10 KB per connection → significant for high-volume TLS termination points (CDN edges, load balancers), calculate aggregate bandwidth. Storage — larger certificates and keys in certificate stores; larger OCSP responses → manageable, plan for 2–5x increase in certificate storage.

maturity_indicators.0: No awareness of PQC infrastructure impact; no testing
maturity_indicators.1: Awareness of PKI/HSM/network challenges; no concrete plans
maturity_indicators.2: HSMs inventoried with PQC status; PKI modernization plan drafted; initial middlebox testing underway
maturity_indicators.3: HSM upgrades in progress; PKI dual-stack operational; all production middleboxes tested; performance baselines established for Tier-1 systems
maturity_indicators.4: Infrastructure fully PQC-capable across IT estate; capacity planning validated at production scale; PKI automated with shortened lifetimes; middlebox monitoring integrated into continuous discovery

common_failures.title: Assuming PQC is a "drop-in" library swap.
common_failures.why: The most pervasive misconception. PQC changes key sizes, signature sizes, handshake characteristics, and certificate chain weights. Every network path, middlebox, load balancer, and TLS termination point must be tested, not just application endpoints; otherwise firewalls drop oversized ClientHellos, IDS/IPS cannot parse PQC chains, or WAF rules break on larger payloads in production.

common_failures.title: Ignoring middleboxes.
common_failures.why: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, WAFs, DLP, forward proxies, and TLS inspection appliances sit on network paths and often have hardcoded buffer sizes or parsing assumptions that break with PQC-sized handshakes and certificates. Test every middlebox on every production network path and create a middlebox inventory as a Phase 6 sub-deliverable.

common_failures.title: Deferring HSM upgrades.
common_failures.why: HSMs are long-lead-time procurements with complex deployment (key ceremony, compliance validation, HA configuration). Waiting until Year 3 to discover HSMs don't support PQC key types causes 12–18 month procurement/delivery/deployment delays. Inventory HSM PQC capability in Year 1 and place replacement orders immediately.

common_failures.title: Planning PKI modernization as a single event.
common_failures.why: PKI changes (new CAs, shorter lifetimes, dual-stack operation) should be phased: start with end-entity certificate lifetime reduction (low risk, high value), then intermediate CA modernization, then root CA planning. Attempting all three simultaneously in a single maintenance window risks outages.

common_failures.title: Neglecting capacity planning for high-volume TLS termination.
common_failures.why: A CDN edge or load balancer handling millions of TLS handshakes per second will see measurable aggregate bandwidth increase from hybrid handshakes. Model the capacity impact before production deployment.

gate.note: Phase 6 exit corresponds to infrastructure readiness gating scaled Phase 5 production deployment; each Phase 6 deliverable (PKI dual-stack, HSM upgrade, middlebox clearance) unblocks a corresponding set of Phase 5 migration targets. Note: Phase 6 is iterative/parallel with Phase 5, so this maps to the framework's infrastructure-readiness transition rather than a single hard cutover.

phases.name: Vendor & Supply Chain Governance
phases.summary: Ensure third-party products and services support the organization's PQC migration timeline. Vendor dependencies are the single largest external constraint on migration speed; vendors update on their own timelines unless contractually compelled otherwise.
phases.overlaps_with: Begins in Q1 Year 1 (as soon as the Phase 0 top-10 critical vendor list is available) and runs continuously throughout the program, escalating in intensity as Phase 2 CBOM, Phase 3 risk scoring, and Phase 5 pilot findings provide more specific requirements.
