Constrains Phase 6 (HSM/PKI/network vendor timelines) and gates Phase 5 (vendor GA releases). Transitions into a permanent BAU governance function — not a project workstream.

activities.title: Classify Vendor Portfolio by PQC Impact
activities.do: Classify each vendor into one of three categories by PQC impact and take the corresponding action.
activities.output: Vendor PQC readiness register (vendor classification matrix)
activities.detail: Strategic Blocking — vendor product is in the critical path for Tier-1/2 migration, no PQC support = migration stops → immediate engagement, executive-level escalation, contract leverage, parallel evaluation of alternatives. Strategic Enabling — vendor product is PQC-relevant but alternatives exist or migration is not blocked → standard engagement, require PQC roadmap, include in contract renewals. Non-Critical — vendor product handles no quantum-vulnerable cryptography or protects only low-priority data → monitor, include PQC in standard procurement language for renewals.

activities.title: Execute Vendor Engagement
activities.do: For each strategic vendor, obtain a PQC feature matrix, GA version and dates, interoperability guidance, performance data, fallback behavior, and CBOM data; drive engagement using the core Vendor PQC Readiness Questionnaire.
activities.detail: Obtain: (1) PQC feature matrix — which products support which PQC algorithms, current vs. planned; (2) GA version and dates — when PQC support is generally available (not beta, not "coming soon"); (3) interoperability guidance — tested configurations with common counterparties; (4) performance data — vendor's own PQC benchmarks; (5) fallback behavior — graceful degradation to classical or hard failure when PQC negotiation fails; (6) CBOM data for the product. Core questionnaire questions: 1) Which NIST-standardized PQC algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) does your product currently support? 2) For unsupported algorithms, what is the GA date and version? 3) Does your product support hybrid/composite operation (classical + PQC simultaneously)? 4) Can cryptographic algorithms be changed via configuration without recompilation, reinstallation, or hardware replacement? 5) What is the performance impact of PQC operation (provide benchmark data)? 6) What interoperability testing have you done with common ecosystem counterparties? 7) Will you provide CBOM data in CycloneDX format? 8) What is your commitment timeline for FIPS 140-3 validated PQC implementations?

activities.title: Insert PQC Requirements into Procurement
activities.do: For all new purchases and contract renewals, add a PQC warranty/crypto-agility clause (adapted by legal counsel) and add PQC requirements to RFPs; adapt existing government model language rather than drafting from scratch.
activities.detail: Add a supplier clause warranting support for NIST-approved PQC algorithms (FIPS 203, 204, and/or 205 as applicable) and crypto-agility (algorithm changes via configuration, not requiring recompilation or hardware replacement), with GA timelines, performance guidance, interoperability matrices, and remedies for failure to deliver by a stated date (maintenance credits / right to replace / contract termination). RFP requirements: Mandatory — NIST-standardized PQC algorithm support with published GA date; Mandatory — crypto-agility (algorithm selection via configuration); Preferred — hybrid operation support (classical + PQC); Preferred — CBOM data in CycloneDX format; Required — FIPS 140-3 validation timeline for PQC implementations. Adapt public model language: Government of Canada ITSM.00.501 and Treasury Board PQC requirements, U.S. DoD CIO quantum-resistant cryptography memorandum, and CISA procurement-relevant product-category guidance.

activities.title: Manage Vendor-as-Blocker Scenarios
activities.do: When a critical vendor cannot provide PQC support within the migration timeline, deploy bridging patterns, run champion-challenger evaluation, escalate contractually, and accept-and-document residual risk if no alternative exists.
activities.detail: (1) Deploy bridging patterns — software PQC overlay (gateway TLS termination, PQC key-wrapping around classical HSM, double-encryption layer) until native vendor support arrives. (2) Run champion-challenger — evaluate an alternative vendor through POC while maintaining the incumbent, and communicate the POC to the incumbent as leverage. (3) Escalate contractually — invoke SLA remedies, maintenance credit provisions, or right-to-replace clauses. (4) Accept and document risk — if no alternative exists and no bridge is feasible, formally document residual risk in the risk register with SteerCo approval and a re-evaluation trigger date.

activities.title: Establish Ongoing Vendor Governance
activities.do: Run the ongoing vendor governance cadence (tracking roadmaps, verifying GA commitments, updating scorecards, reporting to SteerCo, re-evaluating classifications) and report the vendor KPI board to SteerCo.
activities.detail: Cadence: track vendor PQC roadmap status — monthly (strategic blocking vendors), quarterly (others); verify vendor GA commitments against actuals — at each committed milestone date; update vendor PQC scorecard — quarterly; report vendor status to SteerCo — monthly; re-evaluate vendor classification (strategic blocking/enabling/non-critical) — semi-annually. Vendor KPI board (report to SteerCo): % of strategic vendors with signed PQC commitments and dates; number of products with GA hybrid/PQC capability in your estate; age of oldest unsupported critical product (days since vendor committed and missed); number of bridging patterns deployed (indicates vendor gaps being compensated).

activities.title: Coordinate Counterparties You Cannot Contractually Compel
activities.do: Coordinate partners, customers, API consumers, and interbank/B2B counterparties (who offer no contractual leverage but on whom Wave 3 "External, Controlled" deployment depends) using a six-element negotiation pattern.
activities.output: Counterparty coordination (negotiation pattern, feeds the risk register)
activities.detail: Six elements: (1) Readiness discovery — determine each counterparty's PQC posture from observed protocol negotiation on shared connections (passive monitoring from Activity 1.6 captures it) plus a lightweight readiness inquiry rather than the full vendor questionnaire. (2) Dual-stack windows — commit to a published period during which both classical and hybrid negotiation are accepted on shared interfaces, avoiding a flag-day cutover. (3) Deprecation protocol — announce classical-only retirement on a T-minus schedule (announcement, reminder at six months, enforcement date), in writing, through the commercial relationship owner and the technical channel. (4) Interoperability test events — offer scheduled test windows against hybrid-enabled endpoints before enforcement, where failures are cheap. (5) API versioning — expose PQC-capable endpoints as a parallel version rather than an in-place change, so counterparties migrate by endpoint choice and rollback is trivial. (6) The refusal decision — when a counterparty won't move: documented risk acceptance with compensating monitoring, commercial escalation through relationship owners, or termination for connections carrying long-horizon data; the decision belongs to the business relationship owner, made on the program's evidence, and goes in the risk register either way. Sector extensions (Payments and Financial Services) operationalize this for interbank messaging and card schemes.

activities.title: Cloud Shared Responsibility and the SaaS Class
activities.do: Apply the cloud shared-responsibility split (who migrates what) with boundary verification, and treat SaaS as a distinct control-posture class where vendor governance is the only lever.
activities.output: Vendor PQC readiness register (provider attestations + SaaS classification)
activities.detail: The provider migrates what it controls unilaterally (TLS termination on managed front ends, internals of managed services, its own inter-facility links) on its own schedule. The customer keeps everything above that line: application-layer cryptography, customer-managed keys and their KMS key types, workload-to-workload encryption, and every data-at-rest decision from Activity 5.6. Boundary verification: do not mark a provider-side component migrated on the strength of a blog post — capture provider attestations in the vendor register and verify with observed algorithm negotiation at the service boundary wherever visible. SaaS is a control-posture class of its own (not a cloud variant): there is no bridging pattern (you cannot terminate its TLS, wrap its keys, or proxy its internals), so vendor governance is the only lever. Classify each SaaS app in the CBOM by data sensitivity/confidentiality horizon crossed with the vendor's PQC posture (Activity 7.2). For high-sensitivity SaaS with a non-committal vendor, the options are the Activity 7.6 refusal decision applied to a vendor you pay: risk-accept with monitoring, reduce the data entrusted (tokenization and minimization, Activity 5.5), or replace.

maturity_indicators.0: No vendor engagement on PQC; assumption that "vendors will sort it out"
maturity_indicators.1: Ad-hoc inquiries to a few vendors; no structured tracking
maturity_indicators.2: Top 10 vendors formally engaged; questionnaires sent; responses tracked; vendor criticality classification complete
maturity_indicators.3: PQC in standard procurement language; contracts include dated commitments and remedies; bridging patterns deployed for blocked systems; vendor scorecard reported to SteerCo
maturity_indicators.4: All strategic vendors PQC-committed with verified delivery; bridging patterns eliminated as vendor support matures; open-source dependency tracking operational; vendor governance is permanent BAU function

common_failures.title: Starting vendor engagement too late.
common_failures.why: The vendor dependency is typically the longest segment of the PQC migration critical path. Deferring formal engagement until after the CBOM is "complete" loses 12–24 months. Begin in Q1 Year 1 using the top 10 vendor list from Phase 0 scoping — you do not need a finished CBOM to send a PQC roadmap questionnaire.

common_failures.title: Accepting verbal commitments without contractual backing.
common_failures.why: A vendor sales engineer saying "PQC is on our roadmap" is not a commitment. Insist on written GA dates, specific product versions, and contractual consequences for missed dates; verbal assurances evaporate when vendor priorities shift.

common_failures.title: Treating all vendors equally.
common_failures.why: Vendors should be triaged by criticality (Strategic Blocking / Strategic Enabling / Non-Critical). Applying the same engagement intensity to all vendors wastes resources; focus executive-level engagement and contractual leverage on the 5–10 Strategic Blocking vendors that constrain the migration timeline.

common_failures.title: No bridging strategy for vendor gaps.
common_failures.why: When a critical vendor cannot deliver PQC on your timeline, the response cannot be "wait and hope." Define bridging patterns (PQC gateway, overlay encryption, proxy-based TLS termination) proactively so they can be deployed immediately when a vendor misses a milestone.

common_failures.title: The vendor delegation trap.
common_failures.why: Assuming that because a vendor controls the cryptographic implementation, the vendor also owns the migration risk. The vendor owns their product; the organization owns the risk to its data, operations, and regulatory compliance. Vendor readiness is a dependency to manage, not a responsibility to delegate.

common_failures.title: Ignoring open-source dependencies.
common_failures.why: Many organizations track commercial vendor PQC readiness but neglect open-source components (OpenSSL, Bouncy Castle, language-specific crypto libraries) that underpin custom applications. These require the same discipline: monitor release schedules, test upgrades, and plan for version transitions.

gate.note: continuous phase — framework defines no one-time gate

verification_closure.summary: Defines how to prove the migration happened (verification) and how the program ends (closure into BAU). Both are routinely neglected: systems get reported migrated on change tickets rather than observed behavior, and programs drift into an unfunded twilight instead of closing deliberately.
evidence_standard: 1. Observed negotiation, not configuration. Passive monitoring (the Phase 1 continuous discovery infrastructure) must show the system negotiating the expected hybrid or PQC algorithms in production traffic. Configuration states intent; handshakes state fact.

2. Negative testing where classical-only must be refused. For systems whose plan requires rejecting classical-only negotiation (post-transition environments, CNSA 2.0 scope), actively test that a classical-only client is refused. The absence of PQC failures does not prove the presence of PQC enforcement.

3. Certificate chain validation under PQC. For Track B migrations, verify the full lifecycle (issuance, validation by production clients, revocation) operates with PQC or composite certificates. Certificate issuance alone does not demonstrate this.

4. Downgrade and fallback behavior documented. Record what the system does when a counterparty cannot negotiate PQC, and confirm the behavior matches approved policy: graceful classical fallback during transition, refusal after.

5. Evidence captured to the dossier. Each verified system contributes a verification record (date, method, observed algorithms, tester) to the evidence dossier. This converts the dossier from self-reported progress into audit-grade proof.
verification_closure.verification_coverage: Verification is sampled, not exhaustive, for large estates: verify 100% of Tier 1 systems and a documented sample (10–20% per migration wave) of lower tiers, with any sampled failure triggering full verification of that wave.
verification_closure.closure_criteria: Define closure criteria in advance: typically maturity Level 4 or higher across all seven domains; verification complete for Tier 1 and Tier 2 systems; and every remaining item carried as an explicit risk acceptance with an owner and a re-evaluation date.
verification_closure.closure_handover: At closure, execute a formal handover: QRPM transitions to a standing cryptographic governance owner; CBOM and continuous discovery, vendor governance cadence, SOC detection content, KRI reporting, and crypto-agility OKRs transfer to named permanent owners with funded budgets; evidence dossier archived to the records system under regulator-required retention; SteerCo formally accepts the residual risk register; closure decision minuted at the level that chartered the program.

decommissioning.detail: Migration is not complete while the old keys remain. For each completed migration: revoke superseded certificates on schedule (rather than letting them expire silently); destroy retired private keys under the organization's key destruction standard, with destruction certificates for HSM-held keys; remove retired roots and signing certificates from trust stores (a key is only retired when nothing trusts it); remove classical-only cipher suites from configurations once counterparty support permits; update the CBOM entry to reflect retired material. Retired-but-trusted classical signing keys are a standing TNFL liability.
decommissioning.sp_800_88_note: NIST SP 800-88 is NOT cited in this Decommissioning Classical Material section. The text refers to 'the organization's key destruction standard', not to SP 800-88 specifically.

common_failures.title: Declared done.
common_failures.why: Closing on milestone completion rather than verified posture. If verification evidence does not exist, the migration is a belief, not a fact, and the first auditor, regulator, or counterparty who asks for proof will treat it accordingly.

common_failures.title: Orphaned capabilities.
common_failures.why: Treating closure as the end of funding rather than a handover. The CBOM, discovery infrastructure, and vendor governance decay within quarters if they close with the program instead of transferring to funded owners.

cross_cutting.overview: Program Foundations are capabilities that span every phase and operate continuously across the program lifecycle. Five foundational capabilities: a maturity model for benchmarking, metrics and KPIs for tracking/reporting, crypto-agility as architectural end-state, regulatory and standards alignment, and the skills and team structures to execute. Each should be established early (Phase 0/Phase 1) and maintained throughout.

Inputs already exist (traffic volumes from Activity 1.6 passive monitoring; confidentiality horizons from Phase 1 classification). Offered alongside, not as a replacement.

A documented decision to defer is defensible; undocumented inaction is not.

crypto_agility.why: PQC algorithms will eventually need replacement (cf. SHA-1, MD5, DES, 3DES, SSL, early TLS). Goal is not merely to swap RSA for ML-KEM but to build the organizational capability to change cryptographic algorithms routinely. The PQC algorithm set is still evolving (NIST advanced nine signature candidates to round three May 2026; HQC standardized as non-lattice ML-KEM backup; questions raised on specific ML-DSA parameter sets).
crypto_agility.marins_law: Marin's Law on Crypto-Agility: 'The effort required to change cryptography in a system is inversely proportional to the agility built into that system from the start.' Formally: Y ≈ K / A, where Y is migration effort, K is complexity of the cryptographic estate, and A is the agility level.
dimensions: Dimension 1: Architectural agility — Systems designed so algorithm selection is configuration-driven, not hardcoded. Test: can the org change the key exchange algorithm on a Tier-1 service via configuration, without modifying application code, rebuilding containers, or a 90-day change request?

Dimension 2: Operational agility — Tested, documented processes for executing algorithm changes; automated certificate rotation; drift monitoring; tested rollback. Test: has the org executed an algorithm swap drill, changing the negotiated algorithm for a production service within 10 business days?

Dimension 3: Governance agility — An 'approved algorithms' list exists, is maintained, and enforced via CI/CD checks and network monitoring; new-algorithm evaluation/approval documented and executable in weeks not months. Test: if NIST published a new algorithm recommendation tomorrow, how long to evaluate, approve, and begin deploying it?

Dimension 4: Skills agility — People who can evaluate, assess suitability of, and implement new cryptographic algorithms (security engineers who understand the provider-pattern architecture + a CTI function). Test: can the org assess the security implications of a new algorithm within 48 hours of publication?

Dimension 5: Supply chain agility — Vendors/third parties support configuration-driven algorithm selection; HSM firmware updatable without hardware replacement; cloud KMS exposes algorithm selection as a customer-configurable parameter. Test: if the org decided to add HQC alongside ML-KEM, how many vendor dependencies would block it?
principles: 1. No direct algorithm calls in application code (use providers/adapters: JCA configurable providers, OpenSSL pluggable engines, cloud KMS APIs).
2. Algorithm selection is configuration-driven (policy file, env var, or central config; X25519→ML-KEM-768 is a config change, not a code change).
3. Dual-stack capability during transition (negotiate classical + PQC simultaneously / hybrid mode, gracefully degrade).
4. Automated certificate and key lifecycle management (issuance, renewal, rotation, revocation fully automated).
5. Algorithm changes are tested in CI/CD (staging, canary, monitored, rollback-capable).
6. Monitoring of cryptographic posture (detect algorithm drift, expired configs, non-compliant deployments; alert on deprecated algorithms).
7. Approved algorithms policy with enforcement (CI/CD policy checks + network monitoring; unapproved algorithms in Tier-1 trigger remediation).
crypto_agility.roadmap: Year 1 Foundation; Year 2 Adoption; Year 3 Verification (full production algorithm swap drill within 10 business days; measure Agility KPI); Year 4+ Maturation (algorithm changes are routine operational events).

Framework extends beyond CSWP 39 in three areas: Marin's Law (quantitative model), the five-dimension model (vs CSWP 39's primarily architectural focus), and the implementation roadmap integrated into existing phase structure.

skills_team.skills_challenge: PQC migration requires deep cryptographic knowledge + enterprise program management at scale + domain-specific technical expertise — a combination that rarely coexists in one team. Realistic approach: small core of cryptographic expertise, supplemented by upskilled existing enterprise security/IT staff, augmented by external specialists for capabilities not developable internally in time.
skills_team.sizing_heuristic: Sizing heuristic: one dedicated FTE per 500 cryptographic instances in the CBOM for the first two years (discovery, CBOM, risk scoring, and pilot phases). This drops to one per 1,000 during production rollout as processes mature and tooling automates repetitive tasks. The QRPM, Cryptographic Architect, and PMO Analyst are dedicated overhead regardless of estate size.
skills_team.sizing_extras: Team size depends on cryptographic estate complexity more than on revenue/headcount. For <1,000 instances, a part-time QRPM with consulting augmentation for the Cryptographic Architect role is viable. For >10,000 instances, plan a dedicated program office with 8–12 FTEs at peak.

soc_implementation.prerequisite: Every SOC detection capability depends on a single prerequisite: a queryable, continuously updated cryptographic posture registry mapping systems to their expected cryptographic configuration (hybrid / classical-only-pending / PQC-only; expected algorithms and cipher suites; last status-change date). It is a derivative of the Phase 1/Phase 2 inventory/CBOM — the migration program builds it, GRC governs it, the SOC consumes it. Must be machine-readable and SIEM-integrated; designing the integration is a Phase 1 architecture decision.

use_cases.name: Use Case 1: Hybrid Downgrade Detection
use_cases.detail: SIEM correlation rules flag connections negotiating classical-only key shares when the expected configuration is hybrid (analogous to TLS downgrade attacks). Illustrative severity High; FP rate 5–10% in a well-maintained registry. Hybrid key exchanges negotiated via IANA NamedGroup codepoints (not X.509 OIDs); ML-KEM hybrid group values must be added manually (1–2 weeks rule dev per platform). Most common FP source is the org's own middleboxes fragmenting/stripping large hybrid ClientHellos, forcing benign classical fallback; Phase 6 should flag middlebox upgrades.

use_cases.name: Use Case 2: Cryptographic Drift Monitoring
use_cases.detail: Continuous network monitoring flags connections using deprecated cipher suites marked for retirement — continuous compliance verification at the network layer. Alert when an endpoint uses classical-only key share with a system classified 'migration complete'; Severity Medium escalating to High on repeats. Metric: 'Cryptographic Migration Coverage' (% PQC/hybrid vs classical-only TLS sessions, weekly), monotonically increasing toward 100%, regression investigated within 24 hours. Requires east-west traffic visibility.

use_cases.name: Use Case 3: Certificate Lifecycle Anomalies
use_cases.detail: Targets: failed PQC certificate chain validations (Medium); unauthorized certificate issuance during transition — alert on internal-CA issuance using a PQC signature algorithm not on the approved list (High); CA signing key access outside scheduled issuance windows (Critical). Tooling gap: CT monitoring for PQC certificates is immature; SOC may need custom monitoring around internal CA logs.

use_cases.name: Use Case 4: TNFL and Signature Integrity Monitoring
use_cases.detail: Heightened monitoring of code signing events, software update authentication, and systems relying on automated signature verification (firmware updates, financial transaction authorization, identity federation). Alert on unexpected signing keys/identities/times (Critical); modification to signature verification policies in production (Critical); anomalous signing volume beyond two standard deviations (High). Metric: MTD-Signing under 15 minutes for production code signing.

use_cases.name: Use Case 5: Enhanced HNDL-Indicator Detection
use_cases.detail: Same data exfiltration monitoring SOCs already do, with quantum-informed reprioritization weighting long-lived data. Alert on sustained outbound transfers from segments hosting data with secrecy requirements >10 years even below traditional DLP thresholds (High); bulk access to archival storage by accounts that don't normally access them (High). Metric: 'HNDL Exposure Score'; target 100% coverage for 10+ year secrecy data stores, mean detection time under 4 hours. Depends on data classification quality.

soc_implementation.cti: Three horizons — Tactical (hours-days: PQC implementation CVEs, cryptanalysis papers with implementation impact; TTAssess-PQC target <4h); Operational (weeks-months: adversary collection pattern shifts toward HNDL, supply-chain indicators — watch-and-wait as of mid-2026); Strategic (months-years: tracking quantum hardware toward CRQC, national programs, cryptanalytic trends; output = quarterly Quantum Threat Landscape Assessment to CISO/risk committee, feeds the Material Developments KRI).
incident_playbooks: Playbook 1: PQC Algorithm Vulnerability Disclosure (drill metric: impact assessment under 4 hours)
Playbook 4: Emergency Algorithm Rotation (SOC must not mistake rotation for attack; drill metric FP rate <10%)
tabletop_exercises: Exercise 1: The Friday Afternoon CVE (liboqs CVE in production TLS termination)
Exercise 2: The Ambiguous Cryptanalysis Paper (claimed polynomial-time attack on ML-KEM L3)
Exercise 3: Silent Downgrade (classical-only TLS for 72h after load balancer firmware update)
Exercise 4: The CRQC Announcement (Shor factoring 1024-bit RSA in <8h)
Exercise 5: Signing Key Compromise (unauthorized code signing, firmware already distributed)
soc_implementation.roadmap: Phase 1 (0–3 mo): operationalize posture registry, tactical CTI, draft vuln-disclosure playbook + first tabletop. Phase 2 (3–9 mo): hybrid downgrade detection, PQC cipher-suite parsing, drift monitoring, HNDL/DLP review. Phase 3 (9–18 mo): full-scope detection, cert lifecycle monitoring, TNFL signing monitoring, quarterly threat assessment, full rotation drill. Phase 4 (Ongoing): refine.

grc_implementation.why_erm_breaks: Standard ERM assumes observable precursors, historical frequency, established loss models, bounded timelines — quantum risk has none. Timing uncertain (10 to 30+ years); no historical incidents; risk straddles technology/compliance/strategic/operational categories. Fix is adapting the existing ERM framework so quantum risk gets the same structured treatment (risk appetite, KRIs, escalation thresholds, board cadence) as other top-tier risks.

instruments.risk_appetite: Two levels: Strategic (board language) — a single sentence defining overall posture (e.g. complete migration of all >10-year-confidentiality systems before earliest credible CRQC estimates, and achieve compliance with all applicable PQC deadlines with a minimum 12-month buffer). Operational tolerances (program language) — measurable thresholds for HNDL, TNFL, regulatory compliance, crypto-agility. Presented to the board during Phase 0 alongside charter/budget; reviewed annually. Examples: HNDL ≤20% of >10-year-secrecy data on quantum-vulnerable algorithms by end-2027, 0% by end-2029; TNFL all production software/firmware signing on quantum-resistant signatures by end-2027, all CA signing keys PQC-capable by end-2029; Regulatory at least 12 months before deadline; Crypto-agility for all systems deployed from Q3 2026.
instruments.kri_framework: Three-level cascade. Board-level (quarterly): Migration Completion Rate (variance >5pp triggers SteerCo review + board notification), HNDL Residual Exposure (any quarter failing to decrease escalates to risk committee), Regulatory Compliance Buffer (<12mo amber, <6mo red + board intervention), Third-Party Quantum Readiness, Material Developments Flag (qualitative, from CTI). CISO-level (monthly): Inventory Completeness (<80% = unreliable plan), Migration Velocity (<70% two months triggers review), Crypto-Agility Adoption (<95% triggers architecture governance review), Regulatory Horizon Tracker, Vendor Readiness Scores, Budget Consumption vs Plan. Operational (weekly/real-time): Migration Throughput, Cryptographic Drift Count (any non-zero investigated), Hybrid Downgrade Alerts, Certificate Transition Progress, Open Exceptions/Deferrals (>6 months without plan escalates), TTR-PQC.
instruments.regulatory_intelligence: Quarterly minimum cadence (monthly for regulated sectors). Defined process, assigned ownership, structured output. Sources: NIST PQC/NCCoE, NSA CNSA 2.0, EU NIS Cooperation Group, CISA, sector regulators (BIS/BCBS, EMA, NERC), standards bodies (ETSI, ISO, IETF), national agencies. Output: quarterly Regulatory Horizon Report to SteerCo + risk committee, classifying developments Confirmed / Proposed / Signaled and flagging cross-jurisdiction divergences.
instruments.third_party_assessment: Operationalizes vendor exposure ongoing (complements Phase 7). Tiering: Tier 1 migration-constraining (HSM vendors, CAs, cloud platforms, payment processors, MSSPs — detailed assessment + active engagement, require CycloneDX 1.6+ CBOM); Tier 2 cryptographic dependency (standard assessment); Tier 3 no crypto dependency (no assessment). Contractual provisions: support NIST PQC by a date, vulnerability notification, right to audit, crypto-agile configuration commitment. Concentration risk: documented substitution assessment per Tier 1 vendor. M&A due diligence: quantum readiness on the standard checklist.
instruments.audit_evidence_dossier: Internal audit subjects the program to the same oversight as comparable enterprise programs. Audit: inventory completeness, plan realism, migration execution (actually migrated vs marked migrated), risk appetite, KRI framework, regulatory compliance, vendor assessments. Evidence: timestamped inventory DB, quarterly CBOM snapshots, SteerCo minutes, board-approved risk appetite statement, Regulatory Horizon Report, vendor records, exception/deferral register, pilot test reports, training records. Timing: initial within 6 months, mid-program at 18–24 months, annual thereafter; audit observes tabletop exercises.
instruments.insurance: Cyber insurance underwriters incorporate quantum readiness into risk assessments, asking about inventories, PQC migration plans, and crypto-agility at renewal. Organizations unable to demonstrate a coherent transition plan may face higher premiums or explicit quantum-exclusions. GRC ensures migration-program documentation is presentable to underwriters.

grc_implementation.crisis_comms: A quantum cryptographic event is a confidence crisis before a technical incident. GRC owns the external response (SOC owns technical). Maintain pre-drafted templates (customer, regulator, counterparty/partner, market/investor), naming spokesperson and approval chain in advance, exercised in the same tabletops. Expect an attestation surge after any public quantum event; the evidence dossier should make answering an export, not a project.
grc_implementation.grc_soc_handoff: The cryptographic posture registry the five SOC use cases depend on is a GRC asset. Beyond it, GRC produces four outputs the SOC consumes: the risk appetite statement (defines SOC alert escalation thresholds), the regulatory compliance tracker (highest-priority systems to monitor), the vendor readiness assessments (informs third-party connection monitoring), and the exception/deferral register (a dynamic suppression list). Designing these data flows is a Phase 0 governance decision.

algorithms.name: ML-KEM-768
algorithms.notes: Default recommendation for hybrid TLS (with X25519). ML-KEM-512 for constrained environments; ML-KEM-1024 for highest security. On modern server hardware, performance overhead is negligible; on constrained devices, test memory and latency impact before selecting parameter set.

algorithms.name: ML-DSA-65
algorithms.primary_use: Digital signatures (PKI, code signing, document signing)
algorithms.notes: Default recommendation for most signature use cases. ML-DSA-44 for constrained; ML-DSA-87 for highest security.

algorithms.name: SLH-DSA
algorithms.notes: Stateless hash-based; no lattice assumptions. Larger signatures but different security foundation. Recommended as backup/alternative if lattice cryptanalysis advances.

algorithms.name: FN-DSA (formerly FALCON)
algorithms.key_signature_size: Approximately 666 bytes at NIST Security Level 1 versus 2,420 bytes for ML-DSA-44
algorithms.notes: Suitable for bandwidth-constrained environments, though it requires complex floating-point arithmetic to implement safely. Expected to complement ML-DSA where signature size is critical. Draft in NIST/Commerce clearance as of June 2026; final expected late 2026 or early 2027. Do not deploy pre-standard. Plan for it in crypto-agility architecture.

algorithms.name: HQC
algorithms.primary_use: Non-lattice-based alternative / algorithmic diversity backup for ML-KEM
algorithms.notes: Uses a different mathematical hardness assumption (error-correcting codes versus structured lattices). If a future attack compromises lattice-based KEMs, HQC provides a non-lattice fallback. Worth tracking as a diversification option even though it is not yet a final NIST standard.

algorithms.name: HBS (LMS/XMSS)
algorithms.primary_use: Specific use cases such as firmware and software update signing, where cryptographic state can be managed safely
algorithms.notes: Intended for niche, tightly controlled use cases rather than as general-purpose replacements for ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.

cnsa_2_0_algorithm_requirements.key_establishment: ML-KEM-1024 (NIST Security Level 5) -- lower security levels are not permitted for national security systems
cnsa_2_0_algorithm_requirements.slh_dsa: Excluded from CNSA 2.0 despite being a NIST-standardized algorithm -- likely due to larger signature sizes and slower verification compared to ML-DSA
cnsa_2_0_algorithm_requirements.note: CNSA 2.0 is being adopted by financial services organizations as a 'highest common denominator' standard even when not regulatorily required.

regional_variations.stance: Recommends hybrid schemes with ML-KEM as primary; acknowledges FrodoKEM and Classic McEliece as having undergone extensive cryptanalysis
Sovereign algorithms SMAUG-T, NTRU+, HAETAE, AIMer (January 2025 final selections)

additional_signatures_third_round.note: Third Round (9 candidates, May 2026). NIST announced May 13, 2026 that nine candidates advanced. Evaluation expected ~two years. Not for production planning; relevant only to demonstrate why crypto-agility is not optional.

content.intro: Mosca's Theorem provides the mathematical framework for migration urgency.
content.formula: If X + Y > Z, you must act now.

terms.X: Security shelf-life: the number of years the data you are protecting must remain confidential
terms.Y: Migration time: the number of years required to migrate your cryptographic infrastructure to quantum-safe
terms.Z: Threat timeline: the number of years until a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) exists

decision_logic: If your data needs 15 years of confidentiality (X=15) and migration takes 5 years (Y=5), then X+Y=20. If CRQC arrives in 15 years (Z=15), you are already 5 years too late.
The PQCC roadmap distinguishes 'urgent adopters' (X+Y>Z) and 'regular adopters' (X+Y≤Z) using this inequality.
For HNDL-exposed data, X is the data's remaining confidentiality requirement. For TNFL-exposed signatures, X is the remaining validity period of the trust anchor.
content.uncomfortable_reality: For most large enterprises, Y is 4–15 years. For sensitive data with long-lived confidentiality requirements, X is 10–20 years. Most credible CRQC estimates place Z at 10–20 years. The math is uncomfortably tight, and it gets worse with every year of delay.

rows.hybrid_position: Strongly recommended for all PQC KEMs and signatures (except standalone hash-based signatures). Mandated in BSI certification ('visa') contexts.
rows.implication: Hybrid should be the default design assumption in German-facing deployments

rows.hybrid_position: Strongly emphasized short and medium term; Phase 2 of ANSSI's timeline keeps hybrid mandatory for long-term-security claims in ANSSI's visa framework
rows.implication: Hybrid is the safer default for French assurance-sensitive products

rows.hybrid_position: Recommended in the PQC Migration Handbook, especially hybrid-AND internally; guidance, not a legal mandate
rows.implication: Strong guidance toward hybrid, with explicit policy for exceptions

rows.hybrid_position: Prefers a single migration to fully post-quantum PKI rather than an intermediate hybrid PKI; acknowledges hybrid as an acceptable interim measure for confidentiality and interoperability
rows.implication: Use hybrid selectively, especially for key exchange/confidentiality; do not treat hybrid as the UK end-state

rows.hybrid_position: Hybrid key establishment is allowed but not required; SP 800-227 discusses X-Wing as an example general-purpose hybrid KEM

Hybrid acceptable during transition; end-state must be CNSA 2.0 compliant (pure PQC)
Pure PQC preferred long term; hybrid used only where interoperability or resiliency justifies it

content.multinational_recommendation: Deploy hybrid as the default deployment pattern. This satisfies the strictest requirements (continental European agency guidance), preserves interoperability during transition, and provides defense-in-depth against unknown PQC algorithm weaknesses. Plan for eventual transition to pure PQC to satisfy NCSC UK preferences and CNSA 2.0 end-state. This single approach satisfies all jurisdictions simultaneously.

content.intro: Evidence-based responses to the most common objections. Each entry acknowledges the grain of truth before explaining why it is incomplete or incorrect.

objections.response: Confuses the quantum computing timeline with the migration timeline. Mosca's Inequality (X + Y > Z) shows organizations with long-lived sensitive data and multi-year migration timelines must start now regardless of CRQC date. HNDL is an active present-tense threat: adversaries are harvesting encrypted data today. Regulatory deadlines (CNSA 2.0, NIS2 amendment, G7 roadmap) do not wait for Q-Day.

Vendor timelines are set by vendor business priorities, not yours. Phase 7 documents why vendor delegation is dangerous: vendors control when PQC is available in GA releases, not when your organization migrates. Without proactive engagement starting in Year 1, organizations discover vendor blocking issues in Year 3 when it is too late to influence roadmaps.

objections.objection: We will wait for standards to settle.
objections.response: The core standards are settled. NIST finalized FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), 204 (ML-DSA), and 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024. Additional algorithms (FN-DSA, HQC) in standardization do not change the production-ready status of the primary standards. Crypto-agility architecture ensures new algorithms can be adopted via configuration.

Framing it as a standalone budget line is strategically suboptimal. The infrastructure modernization umbrella strategy (Activity 0.2c) positions PQC within broader IT modernization that is independently justified: PKI automation for shorter certificate lifetimes, FIPS 140-3 migration for the FIPS 140-2 sunset, HSM refresh for EOL hardware, library upgrades for CVE remediation. The PQC-specific incremental cost is a fraction of the total.

objections.objection: This is just an IT problem.
objections.response: PQC migration touches every vendor relationship, data flow, compliance obligation, and business process that depends on digital trust. Phase 0 governance intentionally includes business units, procurement, legal, and compliance. Organizations that treat PQC as an IT project discover during Phase 5 that they lack the authority, budget, and cross-functional coordination to execute at enterprise scale.

objections.objection: We will do it during the next refresh cycle.
objections.response: Refresh cycles are typically 3-7 years; some embedded/OT systems 15-40 years. If the next refresh is 2030, the organization starts after multiple regulatory deadlines have passed. The wave-based deployment model avoids big-bang refresh dependencies: migrate via software/configuration updates now, align hardware-dependent migrations with refresh cycles, deploy compensating controls (quantum-safe gateways, overlay encryption) for systems that cannot migrate until refresh.

objections.objection: Nobody in our sector has started.
objections.response: Factually incorrect. F5 Labs measured 42% of the top 100 websites supporting hybrid PQC key exchange as early as mid-2025. Google, Cloudflare, Meta, Apple, and Signal have deployed PQC in production. OpenSSL, Go, and Node.js ship with PQC defaults. The G7 has published a PQC roadmap for financial services. The EU has proposed explicit PQC requirements in NIS2.

objections.objection: We did an inventory -- we are done.
objections.response: Inventory is Phase 1 of an 8-phase framework. Completing an inventory means knowing what needs to be migrated; it does not mean anything has been migrated. The value is in what it enables: CBOM (Phase 2), risk scoring (Phase 3), roadmap (Phase 4), and migration execution (Phases 5-7). An inventory without a migration plan is an audit artifact, not a security outcome.
